name: @lottiefiles/creator-mcp

tools.name: read_scene
tools.description: Read the current Creator scene. Returns scene dimensions, framerate, duration, all layers, current selection, render order, visual bounds, scene-center deltas, and clipping/off-canvas flags. Call this once at the start of most turns to understand what's on the canvas. Use each layer's `ordering` and `layout` blocks to avoid wrong-layer, wrong-stack, and off-canvas mistakes. A layer may also carry an `occlusion` block (`likely_hidden: true`, `occluded_by: [ids]`) when an opaque layer in front of it covers it — treat that layer as INVISIBLE on the canvas (e.g. a label buried behind a button fill); reorder it above the cover with `reorder_layer` before reporting done. No input required — always reads the active scene.

tools.name: apply_keyframes
tools.description:
Add keyframes to ONE animatable property on ONE layer. This is the preferred tool for simple single-property animations (rotate, fade, slide, pulse, recolor). If you need to animate multiple properties on the same layer, plan separate tool calls in the order they should be applied; Creator serializes native tool execution through the dispatcher.

**POLISH TURNS (snappier / smoother / tighter / less bouncy / fix timing / more premium / etc.) — call `read_keyframes` FIRST on every animated layer in scope BEFORE calling this tool.** The conversation history's view of existing keyframes is stale once the user edits in Creator directly; reading is the only safe source of truth. Then prefer the smallest possible mutation: easing-only change > retiming > amplitude tweak > full rebuild. See motion-design.md → 'Repair / polish protocol' for the full rule.

Value type depends on the property:
- `position`, `scale` → value is `{x, y}`. **`scale` is a percentage of the layer's AUTHORED size, matching AE / Creator semantics — NOT a percentage of 100.** A layer the user imported or hand-resized can sit at `50`, `200`, `1250`, etc. — and THAT value is the resting state. Animating a layer authored at 1250 → 110 collapses it to ~9% of its on-canvas size and looks like a bug. **Always read the current static value via `read_keyframes` or `read_scene` before writing scale keyframes**, then animate RELATIVE to that authored value (1250 pulses to 1350, not to 110). Same baseline rule applies to `position` and `rotation` — the layer's authored values are the resting state, not 0/0 or 0°. See motion-design.md → 'Baseline awareness'. **TEXT `position` is doubly dangerous: a text layer's transform anchor is the baseline / box origin, so its raw `position` value is NOT its `visual_center` and NOT the `position` arg you gave `create_text` (that arg is the visual center). Feeding `visual_center` in as a `position` keyframe throws the text off-canvas. For a settle-into-place entrance use `animate_entrance` (no coordinate needed); for any other text move, `read_keyframes` the raw `static_value` and animate RELATIVE to it. Never repair a keyframed text layer with `set_anchor_point` → `center_layer` — they stack two shifts and fling it off-canvas.**
- `rotation`, `opacity` → value is a number (rotation in degrees; opacity 0–100)
- `fill_color` → value is `{r, g, b}` with 0-255 per channel. **Requires a SOLID fill at `fills[0]`** — animation only works when the layer's first fill is SOLID. Gradient or empty layers will fail with `'Layer has no SOLID fill at fills[0]'`. To animate the color of a layer that currently has a gradient (or no fill), call `set_fill({type:'SOLID', color: <starting color>})` FIRST, then this tool. Verify the fill type via `read_scene` (look at the layer's fill metadata) or just call `set_fill` defensively before animating colors on a layer you didn't create with a solid fill.
- `trim_start`, `trim_end` → number 0–100 (percent of path). Use for stroke draw-on reveals: animate `trim_end` from 0 → 100 to grow the path in. A trim path is auto-created on first use. If the current playhead stays at a frame where `trim_end` is 0 or opacity is 0, the layer is correctly present but invisible on canvas; after creating a reveal, call `set_current_frame` to leave Creator on a visible frame.
- `trim_offset` → number 0–360 (degrees around the path). For rotating-around-path effects.
- `stroke_width` → number (pixels). Requires the layer to already have a stroke — use `set_stroke` first.

To set a static color (no animation), pass a single keyframe at frame 0 and consider `clear_first: true` to remove any existing color animation.

Easing is optional on any keyframe; omit it for linear-ish default. Use `CUBIC_BEZIER` with explicit control points for polished motion; `LINEAR` for deliberate no-easing.

Use `clear_first: true` to replace existing keyframes on that property; otherwise new keyframes are merged with existing ones (sorted by frame).

For paint, shape geometry, masks, groups, scene settings, and timing edits, prefer the dedicated typed tools (`animate_paint`, `animate_property`, `create_shape_group`, `update_mask`, `retime_keyframes`) over rebuilding with many generic keyframe calls.

**RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `{ layer_id, property, added, total_after }`. `added` is how many keyframes THIS call submitted; **`total_after` is a real read-back of how many keyframes the property holds afterwards** — it is re-read from the layer, not echoed from your input.
- **Write success:** the call did not throw and the requested value was read back. A non-throwing one-keyframe write with `total_after: 1` is a valid static write.
- **Animation success:** motion requires at least two distinct stored keyframe frames. After a multi-keyframe submission, `total_after: 1` means the write collapsed and the layer will not animate; call `read_keyframes` if the returned count or frames are unexpected.
- With `clear_first: true`, expect `total_after === added`. A LARGER number means keyframes you did not write survived on that property and the result is a blend of old and new — `read_keyframes` before reporting done.
- Without `clear_first`, `total_after` is the merged count. If it is lower than (previous + `added`), some of your frames landed on frames that already had keyframes and replaced them rather than adding.
- Throws (and writes NOTHING) on an unknown `layer_id`, on a property that is not animatable on that layer, and on an unknown easing PRESET `name`.

clear_first.description: If true, clear existing keyframes on this property before adding. Default false.

frame.description: Whole frame number on the scene timeline. Must be an INTEGER >= 0 and <= the scene `duration_frames` from `read_scene` — Creator has no sub-frame keyframes, and a frame past the scene duration is written but never played. Round any computed frame (e.g. a third of a 25-frame beat is 8, not 8.333).

anyOf.description: Explicit bezier control points [x1, y1, x2, y2]. **Only `apply_keyframes` and `retime_keyframes` accept the `{ type: 'PRESET', name }` shorthand; `animate_paint`, `animate_property` and `set_group_transform` need these raw coefficients — they silently downgrade an unrecognised easing shape to LINEAR (wrong motion, no error).** Preset equivalents: ease-in 0.42,0,1,1 · ease-out 0,0,0.58,1 · ease-in-out 0.42,0,0.58,1 · gentle-out 0.22,1,0.36,1 · snappy-out 0.16,1,0.3,1 · smooth-in-out 0.65,0,0.35,1 · overshoot-soft 0.34,1.56,0.64,1 · overshoot-hard 0.68,-0.55,0.265,1.55 · anticipate 0.22,-0.4,0.56,1.

Named curve — prefer this over hand-picked CUBIC_BEZIER coefficients. Presets expand to the exact bezier values server-side. Each maps to a motion PERSONALITY archetype — pick the one matching your Direction and use it consistently (see motion-design.md → Motion Personality):
- 'gentle-out' — PREMIUM archetype (elegant/luxury/minimal): smooth ease-out, 0% overshoot, ~350-600ms feel. The reveal default; spreads motion across the full duration.
- 'snappy-out' — CORPORATE archetype (clean/professional/dashboard): quick, decisive settle, 0-3% overshoot, ~200-400ms.
- 'overshoot-soft' / 'overshoot-hard' — PLAYFUL archetype (fun/bouncy/cute): pop-in / bouncy settle, 10-20% overshoot, ~150-300ms.
- 'anticipate' — PLAYFUL/ENERGETIC wind-up: pulls back before moving forward.
- 'ease-in-out' / 'smooth-in-out' — both ends, cinematic (neutral).
- 'ease-in' / 'ease-out' — CSS-standard, reliable neutral default.

tools.name: apply_motion_preset
tools.description:
Apply a Motion Preset from the user's Motion System to a single layer. A preset is a multi-property keyframe collection for supported layer transform properties (position + scale + rotation + opacity, any subset) with a duration. This bakes the preset's keyframes into the layer — there's NO link semantics, future preset edits don't propagate. Preset trimPath data is not currently baked by the native gateway; use `apply_keyframes` on `trim_start`/`trim_end` for stroke reveals.

Use this when the user names a preset (e.g. 'apply our brand entrance to this card'). For single-property motion (just an easing, just a duration), use `list_motion_system_items` + the existing keyframe tools instead — presets are the multi-property shortcut.

**Mode** defaults to `'replace'` — this is what the user almost always wants. 'replace' clears existing keyframes on the preset's target properties first, then bakes the preset in. Only pass `'add'` when the user explicitly says 'on top of', 'in addition to', 'while keeping', 'compose with', or similar layering language. In `'add'` mode existing keyframes are preserved and the preset's absolute values are inserted with their frames shifted to the current playhead; scale/rotation/opacity are not added relative to the layer's current authored values. 'apply our brand entrance' = `'replace'`; 'apply our brand entrance while keeping the existing wobble' = `'add'`.

Returns `{ layer_id, preset_id, preset_label, mode, duration_ms, affected_properties, applied_properties, readback }`. Success means the target layer was read back with changed, meaningful animated keyframes: at least one applied property has 2 or more distinct keyframe frames. Throws on unknown preset_id, unknown layer_id, presets with no meaningful supported motion, or actor no-ops/incompatible targets where no meaningful keyframes were actually created. If only some preset properties apply, inspect `applied_properties` and `readback` before describing the result to the user.

mode.description: Default 'replace' (clears existing keyframes on the preset's target properties first). 'add' preserves existing keyframes and inserts the preset's absolute values shifted to the current playhead.

tools.name: apply_motion_path
tools.description:
Make a layer's position FOLLOW a path shape — Creator's 'apply path to motion' feature. Each vertex of the path becomes a position keyframe and the path's bezier in/out tangents become the keyframe's spatial tangents, so the layer curves smoothly along the path instead of jumping in straight-line segments between waypoints.

**Reach for this when the user wants a custom curving motion** — 'have the ball arc over the obstacle', 'make the icon trace an S-curve', 'follow this road', 'orbit around the logo', 'fly across the scene'. The path is a regular path shape created via `create_shape`/`bend_shape` (or any existing path in the scene). The motion is whatever curve the path describes.

The tool writes SpatialKeyframes (the same primitive Creator's motion-path editor produces), which is the only way to get smooth curved motion between waypoints. Hand-authoring position keyframes via `apply_keyframes` gives straight-line interpolation between frames — fine for ramps and pulses, wrong for anything 'curve along this shape'.

**Framing — the path must be centered on the scene:**
- Read scene size first (`read_scene`). Set the path layer's `position` to the scene CENTER (e.g. `{ x: 256, y: 256 }` for 512×512). Author vertex positions as signed displacements from that center, capped at roughly ±(scene_size/2 − 40) so the motion stays inside the viewport with a margin (so x ∈ [−216, +216] on a 512-wide scene).
- World motion coords are `layer.position + vertex`. If the target ends up off-canvas, either the layer wasn't centered or a vertex is past the viewport bound. Tangents can extend past the bound — only vertex anchor points need to stay inside.

**Use TWO vertices for an S-curve, not three.** A 2-anchor bezier with strong opposing tangents produces a smooth flowing S; adding a middle vertex constrains the curve and tends to read as a zig-zag. Only use 3+ vertices when the user explicitly asks for a 'sharp' or 'kinked' S, or when the path has multiple distinct turns.

**Tangent rules — get this right or the curve renders as a polyline:**
- Tangent magnitude ≈ 30–50% of the distance to the adjacent vertex. Smaller flattens; larger loops.
- For a smooth pass-through at any intermediate vertex, that vertex's inTan and outTan must be ANTI-PARALLEL — `outTan = -inTan`. Any other combo produces a visible corner.
- For a TWO-vertex S, the start's outTan-y and the end's inTan-y must have OPPOSITE SIGNS (e.g. start outTan = (120, -150), end inTan = (-120, 150)). That sign flip is what creates the S inflection. Same-sign tangents produce an arc.
- See `motion-patterns.md` → 'S-curve recipe' for a worked 2-vertex example.

Prerequisites:
- `path_layer_id` points to a SHAPE_LAYER containing exactly one path shape with at least 2 vertices, OR to a path shape directly.
- `target_layer_id` points to any transformable layer (shape, text, image, precomp).
- Both layers must be in the active scene.

Defaults:
- `constant_speed: true` distributes the keyframes by arc length, so the motion is uniform along the curve (vs. evenly spaced in time, which makes long path segments visibly speed up). Leave it on unless the user asks for 'ease into corners'.
- **`auto_orient`: pass `true` whenever the verb implies directional motion** — 'fly', 'follow', 'swoop', 'travel', 'tour', 'drive', 'race', 'trace'. The target rotates to face the direction of travel for the entire path. Only leave `auto_orient: false` when the user explicitly wants the layer to keep its original orientation (e.g. 'slide along the path without rotating').
- `remove_source: true` deletes the source path layer after applying (the agent typically drew it as scaffolding). Pass `false` to keep the path visible in the scene.

path_layer_id.description: Path layer id from `read_scene`. A shape layer wrapping exactly one path shape, or a path shape directly. Multi-path layers are ambiguous and rejected.

target_layer_id.description: Layer whose position will follow the path.

end_frame.description: Frame for the last vertex. Must be > start_frame.

constant_speed.description: When true (default), space keyframes by arc length so the motion is uniform along the path. When false, space evenly in time (long segments will appear to speed up).

auto_orient.description: When true, keyframe rotation so the target faces the direction of travel. Default false.

remove_source.description: When true (default), delete the source path layer after applying. Set to false to keep the path visible.

tools.name: set_anchor_point
tools.description:
Move a layer's ANCHOR POINT — the pivot for rotation and scale. Mirrors Creator's property-panel 9-grid anchor selector. Compensates the layer's position so the visible rendering DOES NOT JUMP when the anchor moves; if position is animated, every position keyframe shifts together so the motion shape is preserved.

**Reach for this BEFORE animating rotation or scale** whenever the verb implies a specific pivot:
- 'door opens / swings from the left hinge' → `direction: 'left'`, then animate rotation
- 'drawer slides down from the top' / 'curtain drops' → `direction: 'top'`, then animate scale.y
- 'pendulum / clock hand / chandelier swing' → `direction: 'top'`, then rotation
- 'standing thing falls over' (tips on its base) → `direction: 'bottom'`, then rotation
- 'pop in from the corner' / 'punch in from the bottom-right' → `direction: 'bottom-right'`, then scale + opacity
- 'flag flapping from the pole on the left' → `direction: 'left'`, then rotation/skew

**Critical: set the anchor BEFORE adding the rotation/scale keyframes.** Setting it AFTER moves where those existing keyframes pivot — the layer will appear to lurch because each frame's render uses the new pivot but the keyframed values were authored against the old one. Stage the anchor, then animate.

Pass EXACTLY ONE of:
- `direction`: one of 9 presets (top-left, top, top-right, left, center, right, bottom-left, bottom, bottom-right). The gateway maps to the corresponding corner / edge / midpoint of the layer's local bounding box.
- `position`: raw `{x, y}` in layer-local pixels for custom placement (e.g. matching a specific anchor on a complex shape).

If the layer has no clear bounding box (rare — text and shape layers always have one), the gateway falls back to a 100×100 box centered on local origin, so `direction` still gives sensible results.

layer_id.description: Layer whose anchor to move. Must have transform.anchorPoint.

direction.description: 9-grid preset. Mapped to the corresponding corner / edge / midpoint of the layer's local bounding box. Pass this OR `position`, not both.

position.description: Custom anchor in layer-local pixels. Pass this OR `direction`, not both.

tools.name: create_shape
tools.description:
**BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** New layers are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn creates multiple layers, emit the calls in BOTTOM→TOP order — the background FIRST, the foreground LAST. A card background MUST be created BEFORE its content; a sky rectangle MUST be created BEFORE the logo on it. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.)

Create a new shape layer with a vector primitive. Supports rectangle, ellipse, polygon (regular N-gon), star, and arbitrary bezier path. By default it gets a solid fill (`fill_color`, or gray if omitted). For a RING / outline / donut, pass `fill_color: "none"` + `stroke: { color, width }` — that's a stroke-only shape in ONE call. You can also combine a fill AND a stroke. Returns `layer_id` so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes`. If the user asks for several shapes at once, emit one tool call per shape in the intended render order; Creator serializes native tool execution.

**Position is the VISUAL CENTER for every primitive (rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star).** `path` is positioned at the layer origin and extends as its `path.points` define. A rectangle with `size: {512, 512}` at `position: {x:0, y:0}` in a 512×512 scene shows ONLY the bottom-right quadrant — its center is pinned to the scene's top-left corner. To cover that scene the position must be `{x:256, y:256}` (the rectangle's center → the scene's center).

**BEFORE you reach for `fill_scene: true` — STOP. Do you actually need an exported background layer?** Motion-design convention: animations float on transparency so they composite anywhere. The exported Lottie keeps a transparent background — adding a full-scene rectangle BAKES IN a color the user almost never wants in the final file. The three valid reasons to add a background SHAPE LAYER: (1) gradient/multi-stop background that IS the design, (2) contrast genuinely unsolvable any other way, (3) the user EXPLICITLY says "add a background layer". For ALL other cases — including "premium dashboard", "dark mode preview", "card on a tinted backdrop" — use **`set_scene_background({ color })`** instead. That changes Creator's preview tint WITHOUT polluting the export. See motion-aesthetics → "NO BACKGROUND LAYER BY DEFAULT".

`fill_scene: true` is for the narrow case where one of the three valid reasons above actually applies. The native tool reads the active scene's dimensions and sets `size` + `position` correctly. Only supported for `rectangle`.

Parameter shape is a discriminated field — provide the params for the chosen shape:
- `shape: "rectangle"` → `size: { width, height }` OR `fill_scene: true`. Optional `roundness` (px) — set this for ANY card/panel/modal/button; default-sharp corners read as wireframe.
- `shape: "ellipse"` → `size: { width, height }`.
- `shape: "polygon"` → `points` (number of sides, ≥3), `outer_radius` OR `size`, optional `outer_roundness` (0-100)
- `shape: "star"` → `points` (≥3), `outer_radius` + `inner_radius` OR `size` (inner defaults to half outer), optional `outer_roundness` / `inner_roundness` (0-100 each)
- `shape: "path"` → `path: { points: [{vertex:{x,y}, inTan:{x,y}, outTan:{x,y}}, ...], closed: boolean }`

Use one tool call per shape. 'Three circles stacked vertically' = 3 serialized create_shape calls.

size.description: Required for rectangle/ellipse unless `fill_scene: true`. Ignored for polygon/star/path (those use their own sizing params).

fill_scene.description: Sizes + positions the rectangle to cover the entire active scene. **Use ONLY when an exported full-scene background is actually required** (gradient design, unsolvable contrast, explicit user ask). For simple 'I want a tinted preview surface', use `set_scene_background` instead — that changes Creator's preview color without baking the color into the export. Bare prompts like 'design a dashboard' do NOT warrant a background layer; the export should stay transparent. Only valid when shape is `rectangle`.

points.description: Polygon/star: number of points/sides. 3 = triangle, 5 = pentagon or 5-pointed star. Default 5.

outer_radius.description: Polygon: radius to the vertices. Star: radius to the outer points.

inner_radius.description: Star only: radius to the inner points.

outer_roundness.description: Polygon/star: rounds the outer corners (0 = sharp, 100 = fully rounded). Default 0.

inner_roundness.description: Star only: rounds the inner corners. Default 0.

roundness.description: Rectangle only: corner radius in pixels (0 = sharp, larger = more rounded). Strongly recommended for any 'card', 'panel', 'sheet', 'modal', 'button' rectangle — sharp 90° corners read as wireframe, not finished UI. Sensible defaults: chips 8, buttons 10, inputs 8, cards 16, modals 20, hero panels 24. Pills/avatars: use ellipse instead, or set roundness to half the shorter side. Prefer `radius_token` for the standard scale.

radius_token.description: Rectangle only: corner radius from the design scale — xs=2 sm=4 md=8 lg=24, `pill`=stadium (half the shorter side). Wins over numeric `roundness`. Prefer this over a raw `roundness` so cards/buttons land on the system scale. Ignored on non-rectangles.

role.description: Optional. Resolves a DEFAULT slate fill when `fill_color` is OMITTED. 'accent' = slate-700 NEUTRAL default (NOT a chromatic hue — pass `fill` for chroma). An explicit `fill_color` always wins; ignored when `fill_color` is given.

fill.description: Optional named Flat-UI accent, e.g. 'peter-river','carrot','emerald','sun-flower','alizarin','belize-hole','pomegranate'. ONE chromatic hue; purple/violet never (unknown names are ignored). Wins over `role`; only applies when `fill_color` is omitted. **Name collision: `fill` here is a palette NAME STRING — the `fill` on `set_fill` / `set_stroke` / `add_shape_to_layer` is a PAINT OBJECT (`{ type: 'SOLID', color: {r,g,b} }`). These schemas are strict, so a paint object passed here is rejected; for an explicit colour on this call use `fill_color`.**

path.description: Path only: raw bezier points (vertex + tangents relative to vertex) with open/closed flag. Use closed:false for lines/curves; open paths default to stroke/no fill because fill-only open paths do not draw. If you provide fill_color without stroke on an open path, the gateway uses that color as the stroke so the path remains visible.

fill_color.description: Solid fill RGB (0-255), OR the string 'none' for a stroke-only shape. Pass a real object like {r:66,g:133,b:244}; JSON strings are accepted only for compatibility. Omit for a default gray fill.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

stroke.description: Optional inline stroke (outline). Combine with `fill_color: 'none'` for a ring/outline in ONE call, or with a fill for a filled-and-outlined shape.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

tools.name: bend_shape
tools.description:
Bend one edge of an existing rectangle/square-like SHAPE_LAYER by replacing its first shape with a 5-point bezier path, OR animate an already-bent path by keyframing its pathData. Use this for prompts like 'bend the top of this square', 'curve the bottom edge', 'bow the card inward', or 'animate the bend'.

Static bend: pass `amount` (typical 8-24px). Animated bend: pass `animate: true`; the tool reuses an existing bent PATH shape when present, infers its bounds, and writes pathData keyframes directly. Do NOT fake bend animation with scale keyframes. `tangent_width` controls how broad/smooth the curve is; default 60.

amount.description: Bend amount in pixels. Positive values bend the edge inward toward the center. Default 16.

tangent_width.description: Bezier tangent width in layer-local pixels. Larger values make a broader/smoother bow. Default 60.

size.description: Fallback size for the original rectangle if it can't be inferred from the first shape.

replace_original.description: When true, removes the first existing shape before creating the bent path. Default true.

preserve_fill.description: When true, preserves the first SOLID fill by recreating it after the path so the bent path renders with the same color. Default true.

animate.description: When true, animates the bend by keyframing pathData. Use for "animate the bend", "pulse the bend", or "make it flex".

amplitude.description: Animated bend peak in pixels. Defaults to `amount`, then 20.

start_frame.description: First animation pulse start frame. Default 0.

repeat_count.description: Number of spring pulses to create. For a repeated 5s loop at 30fps, use 3 pulses with repeat_interval_frames 50 or 5 pulses with interval 30.

repeat_interval_frames.description: Frame spacing between repeated spring pulses. Default 30.

frames_per_oscillation.description: Timing density for each oscillation. Default 4.

clear_first.description: When animating, clears existing pathData keyframes first. Default true.

tools.name: create_text
tools.description:
**BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** New text layers are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn also creates a card / background / banner, create the background FIRST and THIS text layer LAST — otherwise the text will land beneath the background. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.)

Create a new native TEXT_LAYER with the given content and optional native TextDocument style. Returns `layer_id` so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes` (opacity for fade-in, position for slide, scale for pop). For letter-by-letter or word-by-word staggered animations, emit one text-layer call per unit in the order they should be created; Creator serializes native tool execution.

**Centering is by VISUAL BOUNDS, not layer origin.** Use `center_in_scene: true` for scene center. Use `position: {x,y}` when you want the bounds center at a specific target point (e.g. top-center hero text). Do not manually compensate for text origin/anchor.

**For long body copy that needs to wrap, pass `wrap_width` instead of constructing a text box yourself.** The gateway translates `wrap_width` into a centered wrap box internally — your `position` / `center_in_scene` still controls visual placement. `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment; pass `align: "left"` for a conventional paragraph column. Omit `wrap_width` for headlines, subtitles, footers, single-line text.

Native text styling supports font size, font family/variant or font name, fill color, stroke color/width, alignment, line height, tracking, caps, and `wrap_width`. For "slight tracking", use a small value such as 2-8; values around 20-40 are very wide and can make title text exceed the scene.

**RESPONSE — verify these BEFORE saying "Done":**
- `visual_center` is where the rendered text actually centers. Compare against your intent (`position` or scene center).
- `visual_bounds` is the rendered rectangle in world coords.
- `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.off_canvas` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}`: if any overflow > 0, the new text is clipped at the canvas edge. Self-correct (reduce `font_size`, add `wrap_width`, shorten the text) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

name.description: Layer name (defaults to the first ~24 chars of `text`).

position.description: Visual center target for the text bounds. Ignored if center_in_scene is true.

center_in_scene.description: If true, place the rendered text bounding box at scene center using rendered bounds when available and measured text bounds as fallback. Use whenever the user asks for centered text; overrides `position`.

scale.description: PERCENTAGE, default `{ x: 100, y: 100 }` — matching AE / Creator semantics, NOT a 0–1 multiplier. `{ x: 1, y: 1 }` renders the text at ONE PERCENT of its size (an invisible speck), which is the classic mistake here. Use `font_size` to set type size; only use `scale` when you specifically want a transform-level scale.

font_name.description: Direct Creator font asset name, e.g. "Inter Bold". Prefer font_family/font_variant when known.

align.description: Horizontal alignment. `left` / `center` / `right` are plain alignment — each line is placed at that edge and nothing is stretched; these are what you want for headlines, labels and single-line text. The `justify_*` values FULL-JUSTIFY every line (words are spread to fill the wrap width, so they only do anything on wrapped multi-line text — see `wrap_width`) and differ only in how the LAST line is treated: `justify_left` = last line flush left (the normal book/paragraph look), `justify_center` = last line centred, `justify_right` = last line flush right, `justify_full` = last line also stretched edge-to-edge. When omitted, the layer's existing alignment is preserved (left for new unwrapped text); `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment.

tracking.description: Native text tracking / letter spacing value. For "slight tracking", use 2-8. Avoid 20+ unless the user explicitly asks for very wide spacing.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

wrap_width.description: Max rendered width (in scene pixels) before text wraps to a new line. **Use ONLY when the text needs to wrap inside a fixed-width column** (e.g. paragraph copy, multi-line body text in a card). Omit for headlines, subtitles, footers, and any single-line text. Internally folds the text into multiple lines by inserting `\n` characters at word boundaries — the same hard line breaks 'Shift+Enter' produces in the property-panel text input. The layer's `position` / `center_in_scene` still controls where the wrapped block sits.

Sets COLOR ONLY (not size/line-height — use `font_size` / create_text_group for typography). 'accent' = slate-700 neutral; pass `fill` for chroma. Explicit `fill_color` always wins.

Wins over `role`; only applies when `fill_color` is omitted; purple/unknown ignored. **Name collision: `fill` here is a palette NAME STRING — the `fill` on `set_fill` / `set_stroke` is a PAINT OBJECT. For an explicit colour on this call use `fill_color`.**

tools.name: create_text_group
tools.description:
**USE THIS for any prompt that asks for 2+ text layers as a coherent composition** — hero slides, title+subtitle+footer, label+value pairs, multi-line callouts. One tool call lays out the whole group with sensible typography defaults and centers it on the scene as a unit.

Why this exists: composing the same layout out of `create_text` + `align_layer` typically takes 6-15 tool calls (create each, align each, shrink if clipped, re-center). This tool runs the equivalent sequence server-side with one response, picking Cal Sans (the project default), role-derived sizes (H2 = ½ × H1), and the correct typography color hierarchy.

**Roles** drive font_size + font_variant + fill_color + line-height + tracking when you don't override them (Slate ramp, never pure black; display headings get NEGATIVE tracking so they read tight, not loose):
- `h1` → big bold slate-900 (the main title), tight leading, negative tracking
- `h2` → half of H1, slate-600 (subtitle), slight negative tracking
- `h3` → ~40% of H1, slate-600
- `body` → ~36% of H1, slate-600, neutral tracking
- `caption` / `footer` → ~28% of H1, slate-500 (muted but readable)

If you omit `role`, the position picks it: first item = h1, second = h2, rest = body. So `items: [{ text: 'Welcome' }, { text: 'Get started' }, { text: 'lottiefiles.com' }]` Just Works.

**Sizing**: `font_size` defaults scale with the scene size — on a 512×512 canvas H1 ≈ 44px; on a 1080×1080 canvas H1 ≈ 80px. Override `font_size` per item only when the design specifically calls for it.

**Layout**: `vstack-centered` (the only mode for now) stacks items vertically with `gap` pixels between, centered horizontally on the scene, with the group's vertical center landing on `scene_anchor`. `scene_anchor: 'center'` (default) centers the whole stack. `'top-center'` biases it to the upper third; `'bottom-center'` to the lower third. Pass `{x, y}` for an arbitrary anchor.

**RESPONSE**: returns `items: [{ layer_id, text, visual_center, visual_bounds, ... }, ...]`, `group_visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit` for the whole group. Check `scene_fit.clipped` and adjust the largest `font_size` once if the group overflowed — don't loop guessing sizes.

role.description: Typography role. Drives font_size, font_variant, and fill_color defaults. Omit and the position picks it (first=h1, second=h2, rest=body).

font_size.description: Explicit font_size override (px). Omit to use the role default.

font_family.description: Defaults to "Cal Sans" (the project font). Override only if asked.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

layout.description: Default and only option for now. More layouts will land as needed.

gap.description: Pixels of vertical space between items. Defaults to ~50% of the H1 size (e.g. 22px on a 512 canvas).

scene_anchor.description: Where the group's center lands. 'center' (default) puts the group at scene center. 'top-center' / 'bottom-center' bias to upper/lower third. `{x, y}` for arbitrary.

tools.name: create_button
tools.description:
Build a button / pill / chip in ONE call. Composes a rounded fill panel + a CENTERED label + optical padding (vertical < horizontal) + a WCAG-AA contrast-correct label color + correct z-order (label in front) + an auto elevation, grouped into one animatable precomp.

**Use this instead of hand-rolling `create_shape` + `create_text` + `reorder_layer`** for any button/pill/chip/CTA/tag. It can't get the z-order, padding, radius, or label contrast wrong, and you never have to reference a layer id you're still creating.

`variant`: `button` (md/8 radius), `pill` (stadium — auto-clamps to half the shorter side), `chip` (smaller, md/8). `fill_color` defaults to Slate-700 `{r:51,g:65,b:85}`; pass a REAL RGB object for an explicit CTA color, or `fill_color:'none'` + a `stroke` for an outlined button. Do not pass stringified JSON. `fill` is only an optional named Flat-UI accent string (e.g. 'peter-river') and is ignored when `fill_color` is provided. The **label color is auto-picked** (slate-50 vs slate-900, whichever clears AA on the fill) — only pass `label_color` to override, and it's kept only if it still passes AA. `elevation`: a tier (`resting`/`raised`/`floating`), or `false`/`'none'` to suppress the auto-resting lift. Returns `{ button_layer_id (the group), panel_layer_id, label_layer_id, label_color, contrast_ratio, passes_aa, visual_center, visual_bounds }` — animate the whole button via `button_layer_id` (e.g. `animate_entrance`).

fill_color.description: Solid fill RGB object (default Slate-700), OR 'none' for an outlined button. Pass a real object like {r:6,g:182,b:212}; JSON strings are accepted only for compatibility.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

fill.description: Optional named Flat-UI accent, e.g. 'peter-river','emerald','sun-flower'. Only used when `fill_color` is omitted. Do not pass RGB here.

radius_token.description: Override the variant corner radius. pill = stadium clamp.

padding.description: Override the optical padding (keep vertical < horizontal).

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

elevation.description: Shadow tier. Omit for auto-resting on a filled button; false/'none' suppresses.

label_color.description: Override the auto-picked label color (kept only if it passes AA).

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

group.description: Group panel + label into one precomp. Default true.

tools.name: create_reference_board
tools.description:
Build a whole multi-section REFERENCE BOARD in ONE call — a title plus a stack of labelled sections. **This is the right tool for "illustrate my motion system", a style guide, a color-palette board, a token/spec sheet, an icon or feature list, or any reference overview.** Do NOT hand-place a board out of many `create_text` + `create_shape` calls — that scatters off-center, drops sections off-grid, and floats the title in the middle (the #1 failure mode). This composes everything into ONE `layout` column (origin scene-center), so the board is centered, evenly gapped, edge-aligned, safe-zone-fit, and on-canvas BY CONSTRUCTION.

Each `section` has an optional `heading` and ONE content kind: `swatches` (color chips — a compact bare grid, or a {swatch,label} legend when ≤8 chips carry `label`s), `rows` ({label,value} spec rows), or `lines` (text specimens like font samples or easing values). Returns the composed `layout` result (`items`, `cascade_order` for `stagger_layers`, `content_bounds`, `created_layer_ids`).

title.description: Board title, shown large at the top.

sections.description: The board sections, top to bottom. Each needs a content kind.

swatches.description: Color chips. ≤8 chips WITH `label`s render as a {swatch,label} legend; otherwise a compact bare grid (heading names the group).

swatch_columns.description: Columns for a bare swatch grid (default ≤8).

lines.description: Text specimens (font samples, easing values, notes).

group.description: Group the whole board into one precomp. Default false.

tools.name: set_text
tools.description:
Update the text content of an existing TEXT_LAYER using native TextDocument APIs. By default the tool preserves the current visual bounds center after the text changes, so the layer does not jump when the new string is wider or narrower.

**RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. A string swap can push the new bounds past the canvas edge — check `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}` after EVERY set_text. If anything overflows, self-correct (downscale `font_size` via `set_text_style`, add `wrap_width` via `set_text_style` for paragraph copy, or shorten the text) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

recenter.description: Defaults true. Keeps the previous visual bounds center after changing text.

tools.name: set_text_style
tools.description:
Update native TextDocument styling on an existing TEXT_LAYER. Supports font size, font family/variant or font name, fill color, stroke color/width, alignment, line height, tracking, caps, and `wrap_width` (for paragraph copy that needs to wrap inside a fixed-width column). Setting `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment; pass `align: "left"` to keep a conventional paragraph column. Pass `fill_color: null` to clear the fill override, `stroke_color: null` to clear the stroke color override, and `stroke_width: null` to clear the stroke width override. By default it preserves the current visual bounds center after style changes. For "slight tracking", use 2-8, not 20-40.

**RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. Bumping `font_size` can push the rendered text past the canvas edge — check `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}` after EVERY set_text_style call. If anything overflows, self-correct (smaller multiplier, add `wrap_width` to wrap, or bump the scene via `set_scene_settings`) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

font_name.description: Direct Creator font asset name, e.g. "Inter Bold". Prefer font_family/font_variant when known.

align.description: Horizontal alignment. `left` / `center` / `right` are plain alignment — each line is placed at that edge and nothing is stretched; these are what you want for headlines, labels and single-line text. The `justify_*` values FULL-JUSTIFY every line (words are spread to fill the wrap width, so they only do anything on wrapped multi-line text — see `wrap_width`) and differ only in how the LAST line is treated: `justify_left` = last line flush left (the normal book/paragraph look), `justify_center` = last line centred, `justify_right` = last line flush right, `justify_full` = last line also stretched edge-to-edge. When omitted, the layer's existing alignment is preserved (left for new unwrapped text); `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment.

tracking.description: Native text tracking / letter spacing value. For "slight tracking", use 2-8. Avoid 20+ unless the user explicitly asks for very wide spacing.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

wrap_width.description: Max rendered width (in scene pixels) before text wraps. **Use ONLY when the text needs to wrap inside a fixed-width column.** Omit for headlines, subtitles, footers, and any single-line text. Internally folds the text by inserting `\n` characters at word boundaries — the same hard line breaks 'Shift+Enter' produces in the property panel. Existing `\n` in the text is preserved.

recenter.description: Defaults true. Keeps the previous visual bounds center after changing style.

tools.name: measure_text_units
tools.description:
Return per-line, per-word, and per-character bounds for an existing text layer. Uses the same canvas.measureText pipeline that powers `read_scene`'s `measured_bounds`, but exposes the cumulative pen position per glyph so per-character recipes can place each new layer at the source's exact kerning — no `bounds.width / char_count` approximation.

When to call (REQUIRED before splitting):
- Any per-character recipe (typewriter, per-character-rise, bottom-up-letters, top-down-letters, kinetic-center-build, short-slide-*).
- Any per-word recipe where each word needs its own layer (per-word-crossfade, spring-scale-in) so the rebuilt phrase reads as one centered unit.
- Layout-aware effects that need exact word widths (short-slide-down, short-slide-right, kinetic-center-build).

When NOT to call:
- Whole-layer recipes (micro-scale-fade, fade-through, scale-down-fade, mask-reveal-up) — those animate one layer; `read_scene`'s `visual_bounds` is enough.
- Layers that aren't text — call returns an error.

Returns (positions match `read_scene`'s coordinate system):
- `local_bounds` / `world_bounds` for the whole layer (matches `text_style.measured_bounds` and `layout.visual_bounds` from `read_scene`).
- `font`: `{ name, size, tracking, line_height, alignment }` — pass these to `create_text` per character/word/line to preserve the source typeface.
- `lines[]`: one entry per `\n`-separated line. Each line carries `text`, `local_bounds`, `world_bounds`, and optionally `words[]` / `characters[]` depending on `granularity`.
- `characters[i].local_bounds.x + width/2` is the visual CENTER of glyph i; use that as the `position.x` for the per-character layer.
- `characters[i].advance_x_local` is the pen position AFTER glyph i (left edge of glyph i+1 with tracking applied). Sum across glyphs and you reproduce the line width.

Granularity:
- `line` — only line bounds. Cheapest. Use for per-line recipes.
- `word` — adds word bounds inside each line. Use for per-word recipes.
- `character` — adds character bounds inside each line. Use for per-character recipes.
- `all` (default) — words + characters. Cheap; the heavy lifting is already done.

Limits:
- Measurement uses the active document fonts. If the layer's font hasn't loaded yet, widths fall back to a coarse `0.48 * fontSize` estimate (returned as one-line/zero-words/zero-characters in non-DOM contexts). Verify with `inspect_scene` if you suspect a font-load race.
- The returned positions are in the same coordinate space as `read_scene` — `local_bounds` is relative to the layer's anchor (alignment already applied), `world_bounds` is in scene coordinates.

layer_id.description: Text layer id from `read_scene`. Pass the source phrase's layer id before splitting it.

granularity.description: Which units to return. Default 'all' (words + characters per line). Use 'character' for per-character recipes, 'word' for per-word, 'line' for per-line.

tools.name: split_text
tools.description:
Split a text layer into one new text layer per character, word, or line at exact `measure_text_units` positions. Copies the source font/style to every new layer and (by default) deletes the source so the new layers don't render on top of the original. Replaces the manual `measure_text_units` → `delete_layer` → loop-of-create_text dance.

When to call:
- Any per-character recipe (typewriter, per-character-rise, bottom-up-letters, top-down-letters) — pass `granularity: 'character'`.
- Any per-word recipe (per-word-crossfade, spring-scale-in) — pass `granularity: 'word'`.
- Any per-line recipe (line-by-line-slide, mask-reveal-up) — pass `granularity: 'line'`.

When NOT to call:
- Whole-layer animations — there's only one layer; nothing to split.
- You need different fonts per unit — split with `copy_style: false` then `set_text_style` per layer.
- You want to animate the original AND a split copy — pass `delete_source: false`.

Returns `{ source_layer_id, source_deleted, granularity, layers: [{ layer_id, text, position: {x,y}, bounds }] }`. The `layers` array is in reading order (line 0 first, then line 1, …) so you can iterate with a running stagger index. Each `position` is the visual center of the unit in scene coordinates — already aligned with what `create_text` does when called with that position, so no `center_layer` follow-up is needed.

Limits:
- Up to ~80 units per call. Beyond that the per-create dispatch overhead dominates; consider `granularity: 'word'` instead of 'character' on long copy.
- Splits are sequential, not transactional today — N undo steps, not one. Plan accordingly when chaining with other edits.
- Spaces ARE returned as their own layers when `granularity: 'character'` (their bounds may be zero-width). Skip them client-side if your recipe doesn't animate them, but keep the layer count exact if your stagger formula uses `i` as the index.

granularity.description: 'character' = one layer per glyph, 'word' = one layer per /\S+/ run, 'line' = one layer per \n-separated row.

delete_source.description: Delete the source layer after splitting. Default true. Set false only when you need both source and split copies in the scene at the same time.

copy_style.description: Copy the source's font, tracking, fill, stroke, alignment, line_height, and caps to every new layer. Default true. Set false only when each unit needs a different style.

animate.description: Apply a staggered entrance to the split units IN ONE CALL — strongly preferred over a manual per-letter `apply_keyframes` loop (which is ≈3N calls and easy to mis-center). The stagger reads each unit's OWN resting position, so letters slide into their correct kerned spots. For 'each letter slides up with a 10-frame stagger', pass `{ preset: 'slide', direction: 'up', per_item_delay_frames: 10 }`.

preset.description: 'slide' = move in + fade (default), 'scale' = grow from 0 (centers anchor), 'fade' = opacity only.

per_item_delay_frames.description: Frames between each unit's start. If the user gives a literal number ("10-frame stagger") use it verbatim. Default 4.

start_frame.description: Frame the first unit starts. Default 0.

distance.description: Slide travel in px (preset 'slide' only). Default 40.

tools.name: stagger_layers
tools.description:
Apply a staggered entrance to MANY existing layers in ONE call — each layer enters slightly after the previous, reading as one cascading sequence. This replaces the per-layer `set_anchor_point` + 2×`apply_keyframes` loop (≈3N calls) that the agent used to hand-roll for letter cascades, card grids, list reveals, etc.

The stagger reads EACH layer's own resting position, so it's safe on already-distinct layers (split-text letters at their kerned spots, grid cards at their slots) — unlike `copy_animation`, which would copy one layer's absolute position onto all the others and collapse them into a single spot.

Layer order in `layer_ids` IS the cascade order. Each layer gets a frame-0 hold so it stays invisible/offset until its turn (no 'everything visible at frame 0' bug). Returns `{ staggered, last_entrance_end_frame, ... }` — use `last_entrance_end_frame` to place the NEXT beat (subtitle, button) so the whole scene reads as one composed sequence.

For 'letters slide up with a 10-frame stagger', either call `split_text` with its `animate` option (one call total), or split then call this with `{ preset: 'slide', direction: 'up', per_item_delay_frames: 10 }`.

layer_ids.description: Layers to stagger, in cascade order (first enters first).

preset.description: 'slide' = move in + fade (default), 'scale' = grow from 0 (centers each anchor), 'fade' = opacity only.

per_item_delay_frames.description: Frames between each layer's start. If the user gives a literal number ("10-frame stagger") use it verbatim. Default 4.

start_frame.description: Frame the first layer starts. Default 0.

easing.description: Easing preset NAME as a bare string, e.g. 'gentle-out' — NOT the `{ type: 'PRESET', name }` object that `apply_keyframes` takes, and no LINEAR / CUBIC_BEZIER here. Default 'gentle-out'. To re-ease afterwards use `retime_keyframes({ operation: 'set_easing' })`, which accepts either shape.

distance.description: Slide travel in px (preset 'slide' only). Default 40.

tools.name: animate_entrance
tools.description:
Animate ONE layer's entrance (a settle-into-place reveal) WITHOUT supplying any position coordinate. The tool reads the layer's OWN resting transform and animates relative to it, so the layer settles back EXACTLY where it rests.

**This is the SAFE path for a TEXT reveal.** A text layer's `position` keyframes live in RAW transform (baseline / box-origin) space — which is DIFFERENT from `visual_center` and from the `position` arg you passed to `create_text` (that arg is the visual center). Reusing the visual center as a `position` keyframe value silently throws the text off-canvas (the cause of a 30-call, 3-rebuild logo-reveal failure). `animate_entrance` takes no coordinate, so that mistake is impossible.

Use it right after creating a layer to give it a premium entrance. `style`: `rise` (slide up into place, position only), `rise-fade` (slide + fade, the default), `fade` (opacity only), `scale` (grow from a centered anchor + fade). It only SETTLES the layer to its current resting spot — it is not a relocate, and it must NOT be re-run on a layer that already has position keyframes. Do NOT chain `set_anchor_point` or `center_layer` before/after it. For MANY layers cascading, use `stagger_layers`. For a non-entrance move along a path, read the raw `static_value` via `read_keyframes` and use `apply_keyframes` relative to it.

Returns `{ layer_id, style, entrance_start_frame, entrance_end_frame, duration_frames }` — use `entrance_end_frame` to time the next beat.

style.description: 'rise-fade' = slide up + fade (default), 'rise' = slide only, 'fade' = opacity only, 'scale' = grow from centered anchor + fade.

distance.description: Slide travel in px for rise/rise-fade. Default 40.

start_frame.description: Frame the entrance starts (holds offset/invisible before). Default 0.

easing.description: Easing preset NAME as a bare string, e.g. 'gentle-out' — NOT the `{ type: 'PRESET', name }` object that `apply_keyframes` takes. Default 'gentle-out'. To re-ease afterwards use `retime_keyframes({ operation: 'set_easing' })`, which accepts either shape.

tools.name: list_fonts
tools.description:
List font families available in the active project — Creator's curated presets, Google Fonts, OS-installed local fonts (when permission has been granted), and project-uploaded font assets. Use this when the user names a specific font you're not sure is loaded ('animate "Acme" in Bebas Neue letter-by-letter'), or when you need to recommend a fallback that's actually present.

When to call:
- User names a font you're not certain exists in this project (brand fonts, niche typefaces).
- You're about to call `create_text` / `set_text_style` with a specific `font_name` and want to verify the family + style are loaded.
- You're deciding between multiple style options for the same family.

When NOT to call:
- The user didn't specify a font — `create_text` uses the project default. Calling this would just burn a turn.
- You already called it earlier in the conversation.

Returns `{ families: [{ family, styles, default_style, source }] }`. `source` is one of `'PRESET' | 'GOOGLE_FONT' | 'LOCAL' | 'ASSET'`. If the requested family isn't in the list, fall back to a similar style + tell the user (e.g. 'Bebas Neue isn't loaded; I used Anton, the closest condensed sans available'). Pass `source` to filter to one category.

Note: the catalog is a snapshot of what's currently loaded. Local OS fonts only appear after the user grants the browser's `local-fonts` permission, which Creator does not prompt for automatically.

source.description: Filter the result to one font origin. 'all' (default) returns every loaded family.

tools.name: center_layer
tools.description:
Reposition an EXISTING layer so its visual center lands on a SPECIFIC target point (e.g. a callout at `(180, 380)`, or anywhere off-center). For text, this uses rendered bounds when Creator has them and measured text bounds otherwise, so it avoids the top-left/origin centering bug.

**For aligning to scene center (the common case), use `align_layer({ direction: 'horizontal-center' })` + `align_layer({ direction: 'vertical-center' })` instead — that's Creator's own alignment path and the more reliable default.** Use `center_layer` only when the target is not the scene center. For a brand-new centered text layer, prefer `create_text` with `center_in_scene: true`.

**RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":**
- `target_reached` is the authoritative placement result: `true` only when both an independent rendered-bounds check and the returned `visual_center` match the target within ~1px; `false` when a rendered verification result exists but its center misses, or the returned `visual_center` is unavailable or misses; and `undefined` when no target or rendered verification result is available, including unavailable bounds, verification errors, or the 1,500ms timeout. **If it is not `true`**: retry with `align_layer` (which uses Creator's authoritative alignment math), OR surface the limitation to the user in one short line.
- `visual_center` may be the projected post-mutation center while rendering settles. Use it to understand the returned layout, not as proof that the move landed.
- For text layers the response intentionally omits `position` — the layer's transform anchor sits at the baseline/box origin, not the visual center.
- `scene_fit` also returned so you can confirm the layer didn't end up clipped. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

target.description: Target center point. Defaults to scene center when omitted.

tools.name: set_fill
tools.description:
Set (or replace) the fill on a SHAPE_LAYER. Supports SOLID colors AND linear/radial gradients.

**Picking a default color (no brand defined, no mood specified):** check `list_slots` and `list_motion_system_items` first. If both empty and the user didn't name a color, stay MONOCHROME — Slate-700 `{r:51,g:65,b:85}` for accents / buttons, Slate-50 `{r:248,g:250,b:252}` for surfaces. Indigo / purple / pink / teal as defaults read as AI slop. When the user DOES name a color or mood, pick from the Flat UI defo palette (see `motion-aesthetics` skill) instead of inventing Tailwind values. ONE chromatic accent + neutrals; no rainbow palettes.

**Defaults to replacing `fills[0]`.** Pass `replace_first: false` to append as a second fill instead.

Color stops: each stop has `offset` (0–1, position along the gradient line), `color` ({r,g,b} 0–255), and optional `opacity` (0–1, default 1). Keep stop count modest (2–5 stops typical). For premium 'glow' effects fade the color to pure black and set blend mode with `set_blend_mode`.

**Gradient geometry — `start` / `end` are PIXEL coordinates in layer-local space (NOT normalized 0–1 ratios).** The shape primitive sits at the layer's local origin (0, 0); a rectangle/ellipse with size {W, H} extends from (-W/2, -H/2) to (+W/2, +H/2). The gradient line runs from `start` to `end`; offset 0 is at `start`, offset 1 is at `end`. Common patterns for a centered shape with size {W, H}:

| Direction        | start          | end            |
| ---------------- | -------------- | -------------- |
| Top → bottom     | {x:0, y:-H/2}  | {x:0, y:H/2}   |
| Bottom → top     | {x:0, y:H/2}   | {x:0, y:-H/2}  |
| Left → right     | {x:-W/2, y:0}  | {x:W/2, y:0}   |
| Diagonal TL→BR   | {x:-W/2, y:-H/2}| {x:W/2, y:H/2}|
| Radial center-out| {x:0, y:0}     | {x:W/2, y:0}   |

tools.name: animate_property
tools.description:

**Which sub-object gets animated** — the `property` picks a list on the layer, and `target_id`/`target_index` pick one entry in that list. **Both are optional and default to the FIRST entry**, which is what you want on the common single-mask / single-fill / single-shape layer:
- `mask_path`, `mask_opacity` → the layer's masks (id from `create_mask`).
- `shape_path`, `shape_size`, `rectangle_roundness`, `outer_radius`, `inner_radius`, `outer_roundness`, `inner_roundness`, `polygon_points`, `star_points` → the layer's shapes (id from `add_shape_to_layer`).
- `stroke_color`, `stroke_opacity` → the layer's strokes; `fill_opacity`, `gradient_stops`, `gradient_start`, `gradient_end`, `highlight_angle`, `highlight_length` → the layer's fills, falling back to strokes when there is no matching fill.
- `text_fill_color`, `text_stroke_color`, `text_stroke_width` → the layer's text animators (falls back to the layer itself when it has none).
- `time_mapping` → the layer itself; both targeting fields are ignored.

**RESPONSE:** returns `{ layer_id, property, target_index, target_id, added, total_after }`. `total_after` is a read-back of the keyframe count on the resolved property — treat `total_after >= 2` as the success predicate for an animation. Throws when the property is not available on the resolved target (e.g. `mask_path` on a layer with no masks).

tools.name: set_blend_mode
tools.description:
Set a layer's blend mode. One of: normal, multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, color-dodge, color-burn, hard-light, soft-light, difference, exclusion, hue, saturation, color, luminosity.

Common uses:
- `screen` → glow / shine / highlight layers (fades to black = invisible)
- `multiply` → shadows / darkening overlays
- `overlay` / `soft-light` → color tinting
- `difference` → inverting effects

tools.name: add_drop_shadow
tools.description:
Attach a native Drop Shadow effect to a layer. Renders in Creator's preview and in dotlottie-web (the default Lottie player). lottie-web silently drops it.

Use for: card/panel shadows, button lift, soft glow (distance=0 + large blur), text shadow. **Replaces the legacy 'duplicate dark rectangle behind the card' workaround** — call this instead.

**Prefer `elevation` for UI surfaces.** Pass `elevation:'resting'|'raised'|'floating'` to attach a tuned TWO-shadow stack (a tight contact shadow + a soft ambient one, slate-tinted) in one call — this reads far more premium than a single hand-tuned shadow. `resting` = a card at rest, `raised` = hover/lifted, `floating` = modal/popover. When `elevation` is set the manual color/opacity/angle/distance/blur are ignored.

Manual single-shadow param tips (when NOT using `elevation`):
- `color` defaults to black {r:0,g:0,b:0}. Tint toward dark slate {r:15,g:23,b:42} for premium UI shadows.
- `opacity` is 0-255 (Lottie convention). 191 ≈ 75% (default). 64 ≈ 25% for subtle, 230 ≈ 90% for dramatic.
- `angle` in degrees, 135 = bottom-right (default). 90 = straight down, 270 = straight up.
- `distance` in px. 0 = no offset (creates a soft glow). 4-8 = resting card. 12-24 = floating/modal lift.
- `blur` in px. 0-2 = hard shadow. 8-15 = soft. 20-40 = very soft. Default 20.

elevation.description: Attach a tuned two-shadow elevation stack instead of a single shadow. Overrides color/opacity/angle/distance/blur. resting = card at rest, raised = hover, floating = modal.

name.description: Optional effect name (shows in Creator effects panel).

tools.name: add_blur
tools.description:
Attach a native Gaussian Blur effect to a layer. Renders in Creator's preview and in dotlottie-web. lottie-web silently drops it.

Use for: blurred backgrounds, focus/defocus effects, soft glow with drop_shadow distance=0, glassy/frosted surfaces.

Param tips:
- `sigma` (px): blur strength. 5-10 = subtle, 15-25 = noticeable, 30-60 = dreamy/dramatic. Default 20.
- `direction`: 0 = both axes (default), 1 = horizontal only, 2 = vertical only.
- `wrap`: 0 = clamp edges (default, normal). 1 = repeat. Almost always leave at 0.

tools.name: add_color_overlay
tools.description:
Attach a native Fill effect that overlays a solid color on the layer (multiply-style recolor). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it.

Use for: recoloring imported SVG/image content without editing the source paths, hover-state overlays, themed tints. For shape layers you usually want `set_fill` instead — this is for cases where the layer's intrinsic fill should stay and a color washes over it.

Param tips:
- `color` required, RGB 0-255.
- `opacity` 0-1 (Lottie Fill convention, not 0-255). Default 1 (full overlay).

tools.name: add_tint
tools.description:
Attach a native Tint effect (two-color recolor: dark pixels → black color, light pixels → white color, with adjustable intensity). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it.

Use for: duotone treatments, retro/poster looks, single-color overlays that preserve luminance variation. NOT for replacing a single fill color — use `set_fill` for that.

Param tips:
- `black` color maps to the darkest pixels (default {0,0,0}).
- `white` color maps to the brightest pixels (default {255,255,255}).
- `intensity` 0-100: 0 = no effect, 100 = full duotone replacement (default 100).

tools.name: add_tritone
tools.description:
Attach a native Tritone effect (three-color recolor: highlight + midtone + shadow). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it.

Use for: cinematic color grading, three-tone aesthetic treatments (sepia, vintage, dusk), branded recolors with more depth than `add_tint`.

Param tips:
- `highlight` color maps to brightest pixels (default white).
- `midtone` color maps to middle luminance (default gray).
- `shadow` color maps to darkest pixels (default black).
- `intensity` 0-100: 0 = no effect, 100 = full recolor (default 100).

tools.name: list_layer_effects
tools.description: Return the effects currently attached to a layer, with their ids, types, and enabled state. Call this before stacking another effect, before removing one, or whenever you need to know what's already there.

tools.name: remove_layer_effect
tools.description: Remove a specific effect from a layer. Call `list_layer_effects` first to get the `effect_id`. Other effects on the layer are left intact.

tools.name: update_layer_effect
tools.description:
Nudge one slot on an existing effect without removing and re-adding it. Use this when the user asks to refine an effect ('a bit more blur', 'darken the shadow', 'rotate the shadow direction') — much cheaper than `remove_layer_effect` + `add_*` and preserves the slot order.

**Slot indices** (match the parser order — see add_* tool docs):
- Drop shadow: 0=color, 1=opacity (0-255), 2=angle (degrees), 3=distance (px), 4=blur (px)
- Gaussian blur: 0=sigma, 1=direction (0|1|2), 2=wrap (0|1)
- Fill (color overlay): 2=color, 6=opacity (0-1)
- Tint: 0=black color, 1=white color, 2=intensity (0-100)
- Tritone: 0=highlight, 1=midtone, 2=shadow, 3=intensity (0-100)

Pass `value` as a number for scalar/angle slots and as an `{r,g,b}` triplet for color slots. Call `list_layer_effects` first if you don't already have the `effect_id`.

tools.name: list_themes
tools.description: List the themes embedded in this file. Themes group design-token slots (brand colors, named text strings, etc.). The Default theme is always present; users can add named alternates (e.g. 'Dark', 'Holiday'). Returns `{ themes: [{ id, slot_count, is_active }] }`. Call before `list_slots` if the user references a specific theme by name, or to confirm that any tokens exist before suggesting slot-based edits.

tools.name: list_slots
tools.description:
List design-token slots defined in the file. Each slot has ONE stable id (e.g. 'brand-red') but can supply different VALUES per theme — Default theme might have brand-red as crimson, a Dark theme might have it as burgundy. The toolkit renders whichever value the currently active theme provides.

Use before inventing hardcoded values whenever the user names a brand concept ('brand red', 'primary blue', 'the header color', 'our headline text'). Filter with `type` to narrow (e.g. COLOR for fill/stroke pickers, TEXT for headline strings).

Returns `{ slots: [{ id, type, values_by_theme: { themeId: value, ... }, active_theme, active_value }] }`. Without `theme_id`, `active_value` is what the canvas renders right now. With a `theme_id` filter for an inactive theme, `active_value` may be that filtered theme's fallback value for inspection, while `active_theme` still names the canvas-rendered theme. The `values_by_theme` map shows variants if the user wants to recolor a specific theme. Empty `slots` means the file has no tokens of that type — fall back to inline values and say so.

type.description: Optional slot type filter. Omit to list every slot across every theme.

theme_id.description: Optional theme id to scope the list. Omit to list slots from all themes. Defaults to no filter; use 'Default' for the always-present built-in theme.

tools.name: list_motion_system_items
tools.description:
Read the user's Motion System library — a separate design library from the file's theme slots. Returns colors / gradients / fonts / easings / durations / motion presets that the user has saved (typically synced from Workflow). Use this when the user names a brand value (e.g. 'brand red', 'standard ease-out', 'fast duration') and `list_slots` did NOT find a match — motion system is the fallback library. The values are returned for inline use (set_fill with the rgb you found, apply_keyframes with the control_points you found, etc.) — they are NOT linked tokens. For multi-property motion presets, use `apply_motion_preset` instead of trying to reconstruct the keyframes.

**Hierarchy:** theme slots beat motion-system entries. Always `list_slots` first; only fall through to `list_motion_system_items` on a miss.

**Colors vs gradients — same UI section, two enum values.** The Motion System UI shows solid colors AND gradients together under one 'Brand Colors' tab, so a name the user thinks is a 'color' may actually be a gradient (e.g. a logo gradient saved as `clogo`). When the user names a color and `type: 'colors'` returns no match, ALWAYS try `type: 'gradients'` before giving up. Only declare 'not found' after BOTH lookups miss.

Returns `{ items: [...] }` typed per family (see schemas below). Pass no `type` to get a summary across all families. Order of `animated_properties` on motion-preset items is not guaranteed; treat as a set.

type.description: Which asset family to read. Omit to get a `{ count, ids }` summary across all families. 'colors' returns solid colors only; 'gradients' returns linear/radial gradients (motion-system stores both under one section internally — this tool splits them).

tools.name: link_slot_to_layer
tools.description:
Link an existing design-token slot to a layer's property so the property reads from the slot reference instead of a hardcoded value. Future slot updates propagate automatically (this is the whole point of slots). Call `list_slots` first to find the slot id.

**The link is to the slot id, NOT to a specific theme's value.** Whichever theme is active at render time supplies the color/text. If the user later switches themes, the linked layer follows the new theme's value automatically. You never pass a theme id here.

What each `slot_type → shape_type` does:
- `COLOR` + `shape_type: FILL` (default for shape layers): replaces the layer's fill color with the slot reference.
- `COLOR` + `shape_type: STROKE`: replaces the layer's stroke color.
- `TEXT` on a text layer: replaces the text content with the slot's string. Ignore `shape_type` for text.
- `GRADIENT` + `shape_type: GRADIENT_FILL` / `GRADIENT_STROKE`: replaces the gradient.
- `POSITION` / `VECTOR`: links the matching transform property; `shape_type` ignored.
- `SCALAR`: links rotation / opacity / skew / skew_axis / stroke_width and REQUIRES `property_context`; `shape_type` ignored. Opacity additionally accepts `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` and defaults to `'layer'`.

Returns `{ slot_id, layer_id, slot_type, shape_type }` on success. Errors if the slot or layer is missing, if `property_context` is missing for SCALAR, or if the slot type is incompatible with the layer (e.g. text slot on a shape layer).

shape_type.description: For COLOR or GRADIENT slots on shape layers, which paint to replace. Defaults to FILL for COLOR slots, GRADIENT_FILL for GRADIENT slots. Ignored for TEXT/POSITION/VECTOR/SCALAR slots.

property_context.description: REQUIRED when the target slot is SCALAR; ignored for other slot types. Picks which scalar property to link: 'rotation' (transform), 'opacity' (transform OR fill - see `opacity_source`), 'skew' / 'skew_axis' (transform), 'stroke_width' (paint).

opacity_source.description: For SCALAR + `property_context: 'opacity'` only. 'layer' (default) links the layer transform opacity; 'fill' links the fill paint opacity. Ignored otherwise.

tools.name: create_slot
tools.description:
Create a new design-token slot (motion token) by capturing the current value of a layer property. The slot's value comes FROM the layer — you cannot create a slot from an arbitrary RGB/text input. The typical agent flow is: (a) `set_fill` (or set rotation/opacity/scale/etc.) on the layer to the target value, then (b) `create_slot` to capture it as a named token. By default the source layer is linked to the new slot so future updates propagate.

**SCALAR slots** (rotation / opacity / skew / skew_axis / stroke_width) share one slot type, so they REQUIRE `property_context` to pick the source property — without it the capture is ambiguous and the call fails. Opacity additionally takes `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` (defaults to `'layer'`).

Returns `{ slot_id, type, theme_id, property_context }`. Errors if the slot name is invalid, already exists, or the layer has no property of the requested kind (e.g., COLOR + FILL on a text layer, SCALAR + rotation on a fully-locked transform).

**Slot name rules:** lowercase letters / numbers / underscore / dash, 1–64 chars, must be unique across all themes. If the user gives an unsupported name (spaces, punctuation, uppercase), normalize it (e.g., 'Brand Red' → 'brand-red') and tell them in the reply.

slot_id.description: Unique slot name (becomes the SlotJSON.assetId — also what `list_slots` returns as `id`). Lowercase, digits, underscore, dash; 1–64 chars. e.g. 'brand-red', 'header-text'.

type.description: Slot type. COLOR = fill/stroke colors. TEXT = reusable strings. GRADIENT = gradient fills/strokes. POSITION = layer position. VECTOR = layer scale. SCALAR = rotation / opacity / skew / skew_axis / stroke_width — see `property_context`.

layer_id.description: Source layer whose property value gets captured into the new slot. Must already have a property of the requested kind (e.g. COLOR slot needs a shape layer with a fill or stroke; SCALAR + rotation needs a layer with an unlocked rotation transform).

shape_type.description: For COLOR / GRADIENT slots on shape layers, which paint to capture. Defaults to FILL (COLOR) or GRADIENT_FILL (GRADIENT). Ignored for TEXT/POSITION/VECTOR/SCALAR.

property_context.description: REQUIRED for SCALAR slots; ignored for other types. Picks which scalar property to capture: 'rotation' (transform), 'opacity' (transform OR fill — see `opacity_source`), 'skew' / 'skew_axis' (transform), 'stroke_width' (paint).

opacity_source.description: For SCALAR + `property_context: 'opacity'` only. 'layer' (default) captures the layer transform opacity; 'fill' captures the fill paint's opacity. Ignored otherwise.

link_source.description: When true (default), the source layer is linked to the new slot — future updates propagate. Set to false only if you want to create the slot without linking the source.

tools.name: create_slot_from_value
tools.description:
Create a new COLOR design-token slot DIRECTLY from a value — no source layer required, no scratch-shape dance. Use this when the agent has a `{r, g, b}` in hand (e.g. from `list_motion_system_items`) and wants to register it as a token the user can link future layers to.

**When to use this vs `create_slot`:**
- `create_slot_from_value`: agent has a value, no source layer. Common after a motion-system lookup: 'tokenize the motion-system primary color' → `list_motion_system_items` → `create_slot_from_value`.
- `create_slot`: agent wants to capture a layer's existing fill/stroke/etc. value AND optionally link the source. The traditional flow when the user has selected a layer they want to tokenize from.

**Linking is separate.** This tool only registers the slot. To link a layer, call `link_slot_to_layer` afterwards.

**Current limitation: COLOR only.** Other slot types (TEXT, GRADIENT, POSITION, VECTOR, SCALAR) still require the scratch-shape pattern via `create_slot`. The tool throws a clear error if you pass a non-COLOR type.

Returns `{ slot_id, type, theme_id, value }`. Errors on duplicate name or invalid slot id (lowercase / digits / underscore / dash, 1-64 chars).

slot_id.description: Unique slot name. Lowercase, digits, underscore, dash; 1-64 chars. e.g. 'brand-red', 'header-text'. If the user gives an unsupported name (spaces, punctuation, uppercase), normalize and mention it in the reply.

type.description: Currently only 'COLOR' is supported. Use `create_slot` (capture-from-layer) for other slot types.

tools.name: update_slot_value
tools.description:
Change the value of an existing design-token slot in one theme. Every layer linked to the slot updates automatically when that theme is the active one — this is the canonical 'recolor everything that uses brand-red' / 'shift all opacity tokens by 20%' operation.

**Themes are per-value scopes.** A slot has one id but multiple values, one per theme. By default this writes to the currently active theme (the one the canvas is rendering). Pass `theme_id` to write to a non-active variant — useful for setting 'Dark' theme colors without leaving the active theme. The response's `applied_to_active_theme: false` plus `note` field tells you when the canvas won't visibly redraw (you targeted an inactive theme).

**Provide exactly one value param matching the slot's type:**
- `color: { r, g, b, a? }` for COLOR slots
- `text: string` for TEXT slots
- `gradient: { stops: [{ offset, r, g, b, a? }, ...] }` for GRADIENT slots — stops sorted by offset 0..1
- `position: { x, y }` for POSITION slots
- `scale: { x, y }` for VECTOR slots (scale; e.g. `{ x: 100, y: 100 }` for 100%)
- `scalar: number` for SCALAR slots — interpreted by the underlying property: degrees for rotation/skew, percent 0..100 for opacity, pixels for stroke_width

Rejects type mismatches (e.g. `color` on a TEXT slot) and unknown theme ids.

Returns `{ slot_id, theme_id, type, value, applied_to_active_theme, note? }`.

theme_id.description: Which theme's value to update. Defaults to the currently active theme (what the canvas renders). Use `list_themes` to see options. Updating a non-active theme is silent on the canvas until the user switches themes.

color.description: New color for a COLOR slot. Components in 0–255; alpha 0–1.

text.description: New string for a TEXT slot. Replaces the slot text content; font / size / alignment are unchanged.

gradient.description: New gradient for a GRADIENT slot. Provide stops sorted by offset (0 = start, 1 = end). Each stop carries its color + alpha; the gateway splits them into the Lottie color/alpha track shape.

position.description: New position for a POSITION slot (scene-space pixels). `{ x: 256, y: 256 }` = scene center on a 512×512 scene.

scale.description: New scale for a VECTOR slot. `{ x: 100, y: 100 }` = 100% (unchanged); `{ x: 150, y: 150 }` = 1.5×. Uniform scale is the same value on both axes.

scalar.description: New number for a SCALAR slot. Interpretation depends on which property this slot represents (use `list_slots` to confirm). Units: degrees (0..360) for rotation / skew / skew_axis; percent (0..100) for opacity; pixels (or whatever the property accepts) for stroke_width.

tools.name: unlink_slot
tools.description:
Disconnect a layer's property from its design-token slot. The property keeps its current value (frozen at the moment of unlink) but stops following the slot — future `update_slot_value` calls on that slot no longer affect this layer.

Use when the user says things like 'detach this from the brand color', 'stop using the token here', 'this one should be one-off', 'break the link'. Returns `{ layer_id, slot_type, shape_type, property_context, unlinked }`.

**For SCALAR slots, `property_context` is required** — SCALAR is shared by rotation, opacity, skew, skew_axis, and stroke_width, so the gateway needs to know which property to unlink. For OPACITY specifically, optionally pass `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` to disambiguate between layer transform opacity and a shape's fill opacity (defaults to `'layer'`).

layer_id.description: The layer whose property should be unlinked from its slot.

slot_type.description: Which slot family to unlink. COLOR / GRADIENT need `shape_type`. SCALAR needs `property_context`. POSITION / VECTOR / TEXT need neither.
