shape_type.description: For COLOR / GRADIENT, which paint to unlink. Defaults to FILL (COLOR) or GRADIENT_FILL (GRADIENT). Ignored for TEXT / POSITION / VECTOR / SCALAR.

property_context.description: Required for SCALAR slots. Tells the gateway which specific scalar property to unlink (since all five share SlotType.SCALAR). Look at the slot's label in `list_slots` to pick. Ignored for non-SCALAR slot types.

opacity_source.description: For SCALAR + OPACITY only — disambiguates between the layer's transform opacity and a shape's fill opacity. Defaults to 'layer' when omitted. Ignored otherwise.

tools.name: add_theme
tools.description:
Create a new theme. The new theme starts with copies of the Default theme's slots (so every slot id continues to render with a value when this theme is active). Use this when the user asks for a 'Dark' / 'Holiday' / etc. variant before customizing values.

After creating, the agent typically wants to (a) `select_theme` to make it active, and (b) `update_slot_value({ theme_id, color | text })` per slot to give the new theme its own values.

**Naming rules:** lowercase / digits / underscore / dash, 1–64 chars. Convert unsupported user-facing names before calling this tool (for example, 'Holiday Theme' → `holiday-theme`). If there's a collision with an existing theme id, theme-manager appends a suffix and the response returns the actual id used.

Returns `{ theme_id, was_renamed }`. `was_renamed: true` means theme-manager picked a different id than requested (collision); surface that to the user.

id.description: Requested theme id. Lowercase / digits / underscore / dash; 1–64 chars. e.g. 'dark', 'holiday', 'high-contrast'.

tools.name: select_theme
tools.description:
Switch the currently active theme. The canvas immediately re-renders using the new theme's slot values — every layer linked to a token shifts to the new theme's value for that slot. Use when the user says 'switch to Dark', 'preview the Holiday theme', 'show me what this looks like with the alt theme'. Also useful right after `update_slot_value({ theme_id: 'Dark', ... })` if the user wants to see the change live.

Returns `{ active_theme }`. Throws if the theme id doesn't exist.

theme_id.description: Theme id to activate. Use `list_themes` to enumerate. 'Default' is always valid.

tools.name: remove_theme
tools.description:
Delete a theme and all its per-slot value variants. Slot ids stay; only the per-theme values defined in this theme are removed. The Default theme cannot be removed — that always exists.

Use when the user asks to drop a variant they no longer want ('get rid of the Holiday theme'). If the deleted theme was active, the active theme falls back to Default.

Returns `{ removed: true, theme_id }`. Throws if the theme is 'Default' or doesn't exist.

theme_id.description: Theme id to delete. Cannot be 'Default'.

tools.name: list_segments
tools.description:
List the named animation segments (markers) on the active scene. Each segment is a name + a frame range (start_frame, end_frame). Segments are used by Lottie players to loop / play named ranges and by dotLottie state machines as playback targets.

Returns `{ segments: [{ id, name, start_frame, end_frame, duration_frames }] }`. Empty array means the scene has no segments yet.

Call before `add_segment` if you need to check for duplicate names, before `add_state` on a state machine that targets a segment, or whenever the user asks 'what segments / loops / chapters does this animation have?'.

tools.name: add_segment
tools.description:
Add a named segment (marker) to the active scene's timeline. Segments are reusable named frame ranges — players can loop on one, dotLottie state machines can reference one by name.

Returns `{ segment_id, name, start_frame, end_frame }`. The `segment_id` is the toolkit node id; subsequent rename / remove / select calls take this id.

**Name uniqueness:** segments don't enforce unique names at the toolkit level, but the agent should avoid duplicate names (state machines reference segments by name and a collision is ambiguous). Call `list_segments` first if unsure.

name.description: Human-readable segment name (e.g. 'intro', 'loop', 'outro'). Plain text — any characters allowed.

start_frame.description: Inclusive start frame. Must be >= 0 and <= end_frame.

end_frame.description: Inclusive end frame. Must be >= start_frame. Typically <= the scene end frame, but the toolkit allows beyond.

tools.name: rename_segment
tools.description: Rename an existing segment. Other properties (frames) are unchanged. If state machines reference the old name, they will NOT auto-update — the agent or user must fix those references separately. Returns `{ segment_id, name }`.

tools.name: remove_segment
tools.description: Delete a segment from the active scene. Layer timing and keyframes are NOT affected — segments are pure metadata. If state machines reference this segment, they will break at runtime; clean those up separately. Returns `{ removed: true, segment_id }`.

tools.name: select_segment
tools.description:
Set the editor's work-area to a segment's frame range so the user can preview / scrub within it. Visible only in the timeline UI; does not change the underlying segment data. Use after `add_segment` if the user wants to immediately preview the new segment, or when they say 'jump to the intro segment'.

Returns `{ segment_id, start_frame, end_frame }`.

tools.name: list_state_machines
tools.description: List the interactivity state machines defined in this file. Each one is `{ id, name, state_count, transition_count, is_active }`. Returns the active state machine id separately as `active_state_machine_id`. State machines are runtime configurations — Lottie players use them to switch playback based on events (click, hover, completion). Most files have 0 or 1 machine.

tools.name: add_state_machine
tools.description:
Create a new interactivity state machine. The new (or reused) machine becomes the active one. After creating, add states with `add_state` and link them with `add_transition`. Designate one state as the entry point with `set_initial_state`.

**Auto-reuse of empty default machines.** Creator files ship with an empty `StateMachine1`. If you call `add_state_machine` and one or more empty machines (zero states, inputs, and interactions) already exist, this tool reuses the first one — renaming it to your requested name — instead of creating a duplicate. The response includes `reused: true` and `previous_name` so you can mention it (e.g. "I renamed the default empty machine to ...").

Returns `{ state_machine_id, name, reused?, previous_name? }`.

tools.name: set_active_state_machine
tools.description: Switch which state machine is active in the editor. Subsequent `add_state` / `add_transition` calls operate on this one. Returns `{ active_state_machine_id }`.

tools.name: remove_state_machine
tools.description: Delete an entire state machine and all its states / transitions / inputs / interactions. Returns `{ removed: true, state_machine_id }`.

tools.name: list_states
tools.description: List the states in the active state machine. Each is `{ id, name, type, segment, autoplay, loop, mode, is_initial, transitions: [{ id, to_state_id, trigger?, type }] }`. Returns `state_machine_id` and `initial_state_id` at the top level for convenience. Empty array means the active machine has no states yet.

tools.name: add_state
tools.description:
Add a new playback state to the active state machine. States represent a playback config — what segment plays, whether it loops, autoplay, etc. The state starts with no transitions; add them with `add_transition`.

`segment` references a segment NAME from `list_segments` (not id). If the segment doesn't exist, the player will fail at runtime — call `list_segments` first to verify, or accept that the user might add the segment later.

State names must be unique within a machine (case-insensitive — 'Idle' and 'IDLE' collide).

Returns `{ state_id, name, segment }`.

segment.description: Segment NAME (not id) to play in this state. Omit for a state that doesn't play anything (rare).

autoplay.description: Start playing as soon as this state is entered. Default true for most states.

loop.description: Loop the segment indefinitely. Default false.

loop_count.description: Number of times to loop. Ignored unless loop is true.

mode.description:
Playback direction for this state's segment. Default 'Forward'.
- 'Forward' — plays first frame → last frame.
- 'Reverse' — plays last frame → first frame.
- 'Bounce' — PING-PONG: forward, then backward, then forward… This is the answer to 'make it ping-pong', 'make it go back and forth', 'yo-yo it', 'play it in reverse after it finishes'. Combine with `loop: true` for a continuous back-and-forth.
- 'ReverseBounce' — the same ping-pong, but starting with the BACKWARD pass.

must_complete.description: If true, the segment must finish before any transition can fire. Default false.

tools.name: add_global_state
tools.description:
Add a GlobalState to the active state machine. Unlike regular states, a GlobalState's transitions are checked FIRST every tick, regardless of which state is currently active — so they fire from ANY state. Use this when the user says 'from any state when X, go to Y' or 'no matter where we are' or 'always allow Z'. Adding identical transitions to every regular state is the wrong shape — use GlobalState instead.

**Constraints:** A GlobalState cannot have incoming transitions (the gateway rejects `add_transition` calls targeting one). Each machine can have at most ONE GlobalState — the gateway rejects a second. Convention names it 'GLOBAL STATE' (uppercase, with space).

Returns `{ state_id, name, type: 'GlobalState' }`. Errors on missing active machine, duplicate name (case-insensitive), or attempting to add a second GlobalState.

name.description: Name for the global state. Convention: 'GLOBAL STATE' (uppercase, with space).

tools.name: remove_state
tools.description: Delete a state from the active state machine. Any transitions pointing TO this state are automatically removed. If the deleted state was the initial state, the machine loses its entry point — set a new initial state with `set_initial_state`. Returns `{ removed: true, state_id }`.

tools.name: update_state
tools.description: Update fields on an existing state. Only the fields you pass are changed; everything else is preserved. Returns `{ state_id, ...updated_fields }`.

segment.description: New segment name. Use empty string to clear.

autoplay.description: Start playing as soon as this state is entered.

loop_count.description: Number of times to loop. Ignored unless `loop` is true.

mode.description:
Playback direction for this state's segment. Default 'Forward'.
- 'Forward' — plays first frame → last frame.
- 'Reverse' — plays last frame → first frame.
- 'Bounce' — PING-PONG: forward, then backward, then forward… This is the answer to 'make it ping-pong', 'make it go back and forth', 'yo-yo it', 'play it in reverse after it finishes'. Combine with `loop: true` for a continuous back-and-forth.
- 'ReverseBounce' — the same ping-pong, but starting with the BACKWARD pass.

must_complete.description: If true, the segment must finish before any transition can fire.

tools.name: set_state_actions
tools.description:
Set entry and/or exit actions on a state. Entry actions fire when the state machine ENTERS the state; exit actions fire when LEAVING. Common uses: 'on enter set isPlaying = true, on leave set false', or 'on enter increment session counter'.

Semantics: passing `entry_actions: [...]` REPLACES the existing entry array. Passing `entry_actions: []` clears it. OMITTING the field leaves the existing actions untouched — pass only the field you want to change.

Actions follow the same 13-shape vocabulary as `add_pointer_interaction` (SetNumeric, SetBoolean, Toggle, Fire, SetTheme, etc.).

state_id.description: State id (from `list_states`) to set actions on.

entry_actions.description: Actions that fire when this state is entered. Pass `[]` to clear the existing array; OMIT to leave it untouched. Same 13-variant vocabulary as `add_pointer_interaction.actions[]`.

anyOf.description: Set a Numeric input to a literal number value.
Increment a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Decrement a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Set a String input to a literal string value.
Set a Boolean input to true or false.
Flip a Boolean input (true ↔ false).
Fire an Event input by name (the input must be of type 'Event').
Reset an input to its initial value (works on any input type).
Jump the player to a specific frame. `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '60' or a $inputName reference to a Numeric input.
Jump to a normalized progress (0–1). `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '0.5' or a $inputName reference.
Switch the active theme by name (must match a theme from `list_themes`).
Open a URL. `target` follows HTML anchor semantics ('_blank' opens a new tab).
Emit a custom DOM event from the player host (advanced; consumed by surrounding code).

exit_actions.description: Actions that fire when this state is exited. Pass `[]` to clear the existing array; OMIT to leave it untouched. Same 13-variant vocabulary as `entry_actions`.

anyOf.description: Set a Numeric input to a literal number value.
Increment a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Decrement a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Set a String input to a literal string value.
Set a Boolean input to true or false.
Flip a Boolean input (true ↔ false).
Fire an Event input by name (the input must be of type 'Event').
Reset an input to its initial value (works on any input type).
Jump the player to a specific frame. `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '60' or a $inputName reference to a Numeric input.
Jump to a normalized progress (0–1). `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '0.5' or a $inputName reference.
Switch the active theme by name (must match a theme from `list_themes`).
Open a URL. `target` follows HTML anchor semantics ('_blank' opens a new tab).
Emit a custom DOM event from the player host (advanced; consumed by surrounding code).

tools.name: set_initial_state
tools.description: Designate which state the machine enters first at runtime. Every state machine needs exactly one initial state. Returns `{ initial_state_id }`.

tools.name: add_transition
tools.description:
Add a transition from one state to another in the active state machine. Transitions can fire immediately when the from-state's segment completes (no trigger), or in response to an event like 'click', 'pointerEnter', 'pointerExit' (pass `trigger_event`).

**If you pass `trigger_event`, you MUST also call `add_pointer_interaction` with a matching `fire_event` — or the transition will never fire at runtime.** `trigger_event` is just a NAME the transition listens for; nothing emits that name until a pointer interaction is wired to fire it. A transition with `trigger_event: 'click'` and no matching `add_pointer_interaction({ pointer_event: 'Click', fire_event: 'click', layer_id })` looks correct in the panel but is dead at playback time. This is the #1 way to ship a broken state machine — always add BOTH calls when using `trigger_event`. The only exception: if a previous interaction in this state machine already fires the same event name, you can reuse it.

Default `type: 'Transition'` is immediate. Pass `type: 'Tweened'` with `duration_ms` (number) + `easing` (cubic-bezier 4-tuple) for smooth interpolation between states. Tweened cannot target a GlobalState.

Returns `{ transition_id, from_state_id, to_state_id, trigger_event, type }`. Errors if either state id is missing.

trigger_event.description: Event NAME this transition listens for (a string, not a literal event type). Common conventions: 'click', 'pointerEnter', 'pointerExit'. **If you set this, you MUST also call `add_pointer_interaction` with the matching `fire_event` value, or the transition never fires.** The string here is arbitrary — what makes it work is a pointer interaction emitting the same name. Omit `trigger_event` entirely for a transition that fires automatically when the from-state's segment completes.

type.description: Default 'Transition' (immediate). 'Tweened' interpolates over duration_ms with the given easing.

duration_ms.description: Required when type is 'Tweened'. Tween duration in milliseconds.

easing.description: Required when type is 'Tweened'. Cubic-bezier control points [x1, y1, x2, y2]. Example: [0.4, 0, 0.2, 1] for material-style ease-in-out.

guards.description: Input-comparison guards. Each guard tests one input value at runtime; ALL guards must pass for the transition to fire. Combine with `trigger_event` to require both an event AND a condition (e.g. transition fires only when 'click' arrives AND isHovered === true). Add the referenced inputs first via `add_input`.

input_name.description: Name of an input on this state machine (matches `list_inputs[].name`).

type.description: Input type — must match the input.

condition.description: Comparison operator. For Boolean use Equal / NotEqual; for Numeric all six work; for String use Equal / NotEqual.

compare_to.description: Value to compare against, as a string. For Boolean 'true' or 'false'; for Numeric a numeric string; for String the literal value.

tools.name: remove_transition
tools.description: Remove a transition from a state. Returns `{ removed: true, transition_id }`.

state_id.description: State id that owns the transition.

tools.name: list_interactions
tools.description:
List the interactions defined on the active state machine. Interactions BIND runtime pointer / state events to actions — usually a `Fire` action that emits a named event a transition listens for.

**Without an interaction, transition `trigger_event` guards never fire.** If you added an `add_transition({ trigger_event: 'click' })`, you must also `add_pointer_interaction({ pointer_event: 'Click', fire_event: 'click' })` for the click to do anything at runtime.

Returns `{ interactions: [{ id, type, layer_name, state_name, actions, fires_event }] }`. `type` is the pointer event name (Click / PointerEnter / …) for pointer interactions OR `OnComplete` / `OnLoopComplete` for state-event interactions. `layer_name` is set for pointer interactions; `state_name` is set for state-event interactions. `actions[]` is the full action list in the agent-facing shape (snake_case + natural value types). `fires_event` is a legacy convenience: it's the input_name of the first `Fire` action when present, otherwise `null` — inspect `actions[]` for everything else.

tools.name: add_pointer_interaction
tools.description:
Bind a pointer event (Click, PointerEnter, etc.) on a layer to one or more state-machine actions. This is the wiring that makes `trigger_event` and input mutations actually fire at runtime.

Two call shapes — pass EITHER `fire_event` (shorthand) OR `actions[]` (full vocabulary), never both:

1. `fire_event: 'click'` — shorthand for a single `Fire` action against the named event input. Pairs with `add_transition({ trigger_event: 'click' })`. Match exactly, case-sensitive.

2. `actions: [...]` — full action vocabulary. Each action targets an input by name or carries its own value. The 13 action types are: `SetNumeric`, `Increment`, `Decrement` (Numeric inputs); `SetString` (String); `SetBoolean`, `Toggle` (Boolean); `Fire`, `Reset` (Event / any input); `SetFrame`, `SetProgress`, `SetTheme`, `FireCustomEvent` (no input ref); `OpenUrl` (carries `url` + optional `target`). Multiple actions in one interaction fire in order.

Action type must match input type (Increment requires Numeric, Toggle requires Boolean, etc.) — the gateway validates and errors clearly on mismatch.

**Event input auto-create.** A `Fire` action (whether via `fire_event` shorthand or `actions: [{ type: 'Fire', input_name: 'X' }]`) needs an Event input named `X` to receive the fire — otherwise the fire vanishes and transitions listening for `X` never trigger. To keep this one-call, the gateway AUTO-CREATES any missing Event inputs referenced by Fire actions. The response includes an `auto_created_inputs` array when this happens, so you can surface it to the user (e.g. "Created event input `click` and wired the click handler.").

Returns `{ interaction_id, pointer_event, fire_event?, actions?, layer_id, layer_name, auto_created_inputs? }`.

pointer_event.description: Which pointer interaction fires this event. Click + PointerEnter / PointerExit are the most common.

fire_event.description: SHORTHAND for a single Fire action. Event name to emit; must match the `trigger_event` you used on a transition (case-sensitive). Common values: 'click', 'hover', 'leave'. Mutually exclusive with `actions[]` — pass one or the other, not both.

actions.description: Full action vocabulary. Mutually exclusive with `fire_event`. Each entry is one of the 13 action variants below; multiple actions fire in order. Must contain at least one action.

anyOf.description: Set a Numeric input to a literal number value.
Increment a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Decrement a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Set a String input to a literal string value.
Set a Boolean input to true or false.
Flip a Boolean input (true ↔ false).
Fire an Event input by name (the input must be of type 'Event'). The shorthand `fire_event` field on this tool is sugar for a single Fire action.
Reset an input to its initial value (works on any input type).
Jump the player to a specific frame. `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '60' or a $inputName reference to a Numeric input (e.g. '$progress').
Jump to a normalized progress (0–1). `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '0.5' or a $inputName reference.
Switch the active theme by name (must match a theme from `list_themes`).
Open a URL. `target` follows HTML anchor semantics ('_blank' opens a new tab).
Emit a custom DOM event from the player host (advanced; consumed by surrounding code).

layer_id.description: Layer id to bind the pointer event to (from `read_scene`). REQUIRED — scene-level pointer interactions don't fire in the player. Pick the most semantically meaningful clickable layer (a button, a card, the whole hero element).

tools.name: add_state_interaction
tools.description:
Add a state-event interaction that fires actions when a state's playback reaches a milestone. Use `OnComplete` for 'when this state's segment finishes' or `OnLoopComplete` for 'each time this state's segment loops'.

Not to be confused with `add_transition`: a transition WITHOUT `trigger_event` also fires on segment completion, but it transitions to ANOTHER state. Use `add_state_interaction` when you want to fire actions (Fire, Increment, SetTheme, OpenUrl, etc.) on completion WITHOUT changing state.

The action vocabulary is identical to `add_pointer_interaction.actions[]` — 13 variants covering input mutations (SetNumeric, Increment, Toggle, …), playback (SetFrame, SetProgress), theme (SetTheme), and side effects (OpenUrl, FireCustomEvent). Action type must match input type or the gateway errors clearly.

**Event input auto-create.** Like `add_pointer_interaction`, this tool auto-creates any Event input referenced by a `Fire` action that doesn't yet exist on the active machine. The response includes `auto_created_inputs` when this happens.

Returns `{ interaction_id, trigger, state_id, state_name, actions, auto_created_inputs? }`.

trigger.description: Which playback milestone fires this interaction. `OnComplete` fires once when the state's segment ends. `OnLoopComplete` fires every time the segment loops back.

state_id.description: State id (from `list_states`) whose milestone fires the interaction.

actions.description: Actions to fire when the trigger hits. Same 13-variant vocabulary as `add_pointer_interaction.actions[]`. Multiple actions fire in order. Must contain at least one action.

anyOf.description: Set a Numeric input to a literal number value.
Increment a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Decrement a Numeric input by `value` (defaults to 1).
Set a String input to a literal string value.
Set a Boolean input to true or false.
Flip a Boolean input (true ↔ false).
Fire an Event input by name (the input must be of type 'Event').
Reset an input to its initial value (works on any input type).
Jump the player to a specific frame. `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '60' or a $inputName reference to a Numeric input (e.g. '$progress').
Jump to a normalized progress (0–1). `value` is a string — a numeric literal like '0.5' or a $inputName reference.
Switch the active theme by name (must match a theme from `list_themes`).
Open a URL. `target` follows HTML anchor semantics ('_blank' opens a new tab).
Emit a custom DOM event from the player host (advanced; consumed by surrounding code).

tools.name: remove_interaction
tools.description: Remove an interaction from the active state machine. Returns `{ removed: true, interaction_id }`.

tools.name: list_inputs
tools.description:
List the typed inputs (variables) on the active state machine. Inputs are how state machines store runtime values — booleans for toggle state, numerics for progress / counters, strings for labels, and events for one-shot triggers. Inputs feed guards on transitions and actions in interactions.

Returns `{ inputs: [{ id, name, type, value? }] }`. The `value` is the initial value at machine start (events don't have one).

tools.name: add_input
tools.description:
Add a typed input variable to the active state machine. Inputs power guard transitions (e.g. transition fires when `isHovered === true`) and action targets (e.g. an action that sets `progress` to 50).

Types:
- `Boolean` — initial_value must be 'true' or 'false' (string).
- `Numeric` — initial_value must be a stringified number.
- `String` — initial_value is a plain string.
- `Event` — pure one-shot trigger; do not pass initial_value.

Returns `{ input_id, name, type }`.

name.description: Variable name — referenced by guards and actions. e.g. 'isHovered', 'progress', 'currentTab'.

type.description: Input type. Boolean for toggles, Numeric for counters/progress, String for labels, Event for one-shot triggers.

initial_value.description: Initial value as a string. For Boolean pass 'true' or 'false'; for Numeric pass a numeric string like '0'; for String any text; OMIT for Event.

tools.name: update_input
tools.description: Update an existing input's name or value. Renaming an input also updates all references to it across guards and actions automatically (theme-manager handles the cascade). Returns `{ input_id, name, value }`.

value.description: New value as a string (matches the input type).

tools.name: remove_input
tools.description: Delete an input. All guards / actions that reference it are also cleaned up automatically. Returns `{ removed: true, input_id }`.

tools.name: import_asset
tools.description:
**BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** Imported assets are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn creates multiple layers, emit the calls in BOTTOM→TOP order — the backdrop / sky / base image FIRST, foreground layers LAST. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.)

Import an SVG, Lottie, or image into the active scene as a new layer. This is the preferred tool whenever the user pastes SVG markup, provides a URL for an image/Lottie, or asks to add an existing asset. Returns the new layer's id so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes`.

Provide either `content` (for inline SVG markup) or `url` (for Lottie JSON / image URLs). Optional `name`, `position`, and `scale` are applied after import.

asset_type.description: SVG: use inline `content`. LOTTIE/IMAGE: use `url`. Inline SVG content is the common case when the user pastes markup.

content.description: Raw SVG markup (for asset_type='SVG'). Mutually exclusive with `url`.

url.description: URL to fetch (for asset_type='LOTTIE' or 'IMAGE'). Mutually exclusive with `content`.

name.description: Optional override for the imported layer's name.

position.description: Optional {x, y} to position the imported layer.

tools.name: vectorize_image
tools.description: Convert an existing PNG/JPG image layer into editable vector shape layers using Creator's vectorizer. Use this when the user asks to vectorize, trace, convert an image/logo/photo to vectors, or make an imported raster image editable. Defaults to the selected image layer when `layer_id` is omitted. The generated vector layers are inserted above the source and selected; after at least one vector layer is created, the original raster is preserved but hidden so it does not render or export twice. Restore it with `set_layer_visibility({ layer_id: source_layer_id, visible: true })` when the user wants to compare or revert.

layer_id.description: Image layer id from `read_scene`. Optional when an image layer is selected.

tools.name: remove_keyframes
tools.description: Remove keyframes from a single property on a single layer. Omit `frame_range` to clear all keyframes on that property; pass `frame_range: { from, to }` to remove only keyframes whose frame falls in the inclusive range. Use this before calling `apply_keyframes` with the same property when you want to fully replace an existing animation rather than merge with it — or just pass `clear_first: true` on `apply_keyframes` for the common case.

tools.name: duplicate_layer
tools.description:
Duplicate an existing layer N times and return the new layer IDs. Optional `stagger_frames` offsets each duplicate's timelineOffset by that many frames (i × stagger) — use for stagger/wave effects. Optional `offset` shifts each duplicate's position by (i × offset.x, i × offset.y) — use for arrays and rows.

Common flows:
- 'make a row of 5 dots spaced 40px apart': duplicate_layer with count=4 (+ the source = 5 total) and offset={x:40,y:0}, then a single apply_keyframes call on the source animates the base motion.
- 'stagger 5 letters': duplicate_layer with count=4 and stagger_frames=3; each clone gets timelineOffset = source + i*3.
- **2-D grid (rows × cols)**: call duplicate_layer once per row — first call with count=cols-1 and offset={x:tile,y:0} (top row), then for each additional row, call with count=cols-1 on ONE of the top-row tiles and offset={x:0,y:tile}. Or simpler: N serialized calls, one per row, each duplicating a source tile with x-offsets. Do NOT attempt a 2-D grid with a single duplicate_layer call — `offset` is 1-D.

Returns an array of `{ layer_id, name }` for the new layers, in creation order. Capped at 24 copies per call.

count.description: How many duplicates to create. Default 1. Capped at 24 to keep the timeline sane.

stagger_frames.description: Per-copy timelineOffset step, in frames. Copy i (1-indexed) gets source.timelineOffset + i*stagger_frames.

offset.description: Per-copy position shift. Copy i gets source.position + i*offset. Ignored if the source layer has animated position (copy keyframes untouched).

name_prefix.description: Optional base name. Copies are suffixed ' 1', ' 2', etc. Defaults to the source layer's name.

tools.name: tile_layer
tools.description:
Fill the active scene with a grid of copies of a layer. This is the tool to reach for whenever the user says 'tile across the scene', 'fill with a grid of', 'cover with', 'scatter N', or 'pattern the background with'. It ALWAYS uses `Math.floor` for auto cols/rows so tiles never spill outside the scene bounds.

Behavior:
- `tile_width` / `tile_height` default to the source layer's visual bounds (read via getBounds). For a polygon with outerRadius 50, that's ~100×100.
- `cols` / `rows` default to `floor((scene_dim − 2*margin + gap) / (tile_dim + gap))` so the grid exactly fits. Pass either explicitly to override.
- Grid is centered inside the `margin`-inset scene rect.
- Optional `gap` between tiles (default 0).
- Optional `margin` (default 0) to inset the grid from scene edges.
- Optional `alternate_flip: true` rotates odd rows by 180° — ideal for triangle tessellation.
- Reuses the source layer as cell (0,0); only cols×rows−1 new layers are created.
- Hard cap of 144 tiles (12×12) to keep Creator responsive. Throws if exceeded.

Example: 'tile this triangle to fill the scene' → one call, no params beyond layer_id. For a 512×512 scene with a 100px triangle: fills as 5×5 with the grid centered.

layer_id.description: Source layer to duplicate into the grid.

cols.description: Explicit column count. Omit to auto-fit from tile_width + margin + gap.

rows.description: Explicit row count. Omit to auto-fit.

tile_width.description: Override the per-tile width step. Defaults to the source layer's visual bounds width (via getBounds).

tile_height.description: Override the per-tile height step. Defaults to source bounds height.

gap.description: Spacing between tiles in pixels. Default { x: 0, y: 0 } (tiles touch).

margin.description: Inset from scene edges in pixels. Default { x: 0, y: 0 }.

alternate_flip.description: When true, rotate odd-indexed rows by 180°. Use for triangle tessellation and pointing alternating directions.

tools.name: reorder_layer
tools.description:
Restack a layer relative to another in the active scene's render order. Use when creation order was wrong or the user asks to put one layer above/below/in-front-of/behind another.

Z-ORDER (index 0 = front/top, per read_scene `ordering`):
- To put the layer ON TOP of the sibling (visible in front — e.g. a label over a button fill, text over a circle): `position: 'in_front_of'`.
- To put the layer UNDER the sibling (behind — e.g. a shadow behind a card, a backdrop behind content): `position: 'behind'`.

USE `in_front_of` / `behind` — they say exactly what you mean. The legacy `before` / `after` refer to render-ARRAY position and invert intuitively (`before` the sibling = drawn after it = renders ON TOP); only use them if you're certain. "bring to front" = `in_front_of` the current front layer; "send to back" = `behind` the current back layer.

Pass `layer_id` (the layer to move), `sibling_layer_id` (stays put), `position`. The canvas re-renders after the move — verify with `inspect_scene` and check the target isn't `occlusion.likely_hidden`.

sibling_layer_id.description: Reference layer that stays in place; the target moves relative to it.

position.description: Where to place the target relative to the sibling. `in_front_of` = on top (visible over it); `behind` = under it. (`before` = same as in_front_of, `after` = same as behind — legacy, easy to invert.)

tools.name: group_layers
tools.description: Group multiple active-scene root layers by converting them into a nestable precomposition layer. Creator's native shape-group command only groups drawable shapes inside a shape layer, so root-level layer grouping is represented as a precomp. Use this when the user asks to group several layers, package a component, or create a reusable/nestable precomp from existing layers. Pass layer IDs from `read_scene` in the intended visual set.

name.description: Optional name for the resulting precomposition layer.

tools.name: create_shape_group
tools.description:
Create an empty group inside an existing SHAPE_LAYER or group. Use this to build composed single-layer components like cards, icons, badges, and shadows without creating many top-level layers.

**RESPONSE — keep `group_id`, it is the only way to address the group afterwards:** returns `{ group_id, parent_id, name }`. `read_scene` returns LAYERS, not the shape/group tree inside them, so this response is your only source of the id. Feed `group_id` straight into `add_shape_to_layer({ parent_id: group_id })` to fill the group and into `set_group_transform({ group_id })` to move / fade the whole group as one unit.

parent_id.description: Container to create the group inside: a SHAPE_LAYER id (the `layer_id` returned by `create_shape`) or another group id (a `group_id` returned by an earlier `create_shape_group`). Non-shape layers are rejected.

name.description: Optional group name, e.g. "card-shadow". Defaults to Creator's.

tools.name: add_shape_to_layer
tools.description:
Add a rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star, or path to an existing SHAPE_LAYER or group. Use with create_shape_group to build one composed unit with internal groups.

**RESPONSE:** returns `{ parent_id, shape_id, shape, fill_id, stroke_id }` (`fill_id` / `stroke_id` only when you passed `fill` / `stroke`). Keep `shape_id` — it is the `target_id` for `animate_property` on shape geometry (`shape_size`, `rectangle_roundness`, `shape_path`, …), and `read_scene` does not list the shapes inside a layer. If the fill or stroke fails to attach, the whole call is rolled back (the shape is removed) and it throws, so a successful response means every requested piece exists.

parent_id.description: Container to add the shape to: a SHAPE_LAYER id (from `create_shape`) or a `group_id` from `create_shape_group`.

fill.description: PAINT OBJECT — `{ type: 'SOLID', color: {r,g,b} }` or a gradient, same shape as `set_fill.fill`. NOT the palette NAME STRING that `create_shape.fill` takes.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

stroke.description: PAINT OBJECT plus an optional `width` (px, default 1) — e.g. `{ type: 'SOLID', color: {r,g,b}, width: 2 }`. NOT the `{ color, width }` shape that `create_shape.stroke` takes.

anyOf.description: Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.
Compatibility only: JSON-stringified RGB object. Prefer a real {r,g,b} object.

tools.name: set_group_transform
tools.description:
Set or keyframe a shape group transform/opacity property. Use this when a composed unit has internal groups that should move or fade together.

Pass EITHER `value` (a static set) OR `keyframes` (an animation) — the call throws if you pass neither. `keyframes` wins when both are given.

Returns `{ group_id, property, keyframes_added }`; `keyframes_added` is 0 for a static `value` set.

group_id.description: Group id from the `create_shape_group` response. `read_scene` lists layers, not the groups inside them, so that response (or an earlier `add_shape_to_layer` parent) is where this id comes from.

value.description: Static value to set (no animation). `{x, y}` for position/scale, a number for rotation (degrees) / opacity (0-100). Omit when passing `keyframes`.

clear_first.description: Clear existing keyframes on this group property before writing. **Defaults to TRUE here** (unlike `apply_keyframes`, which defaults to false). Pass false to merge with what is already there.

anyOf.description: Explicit bezier control points [x1, y1, x2, y2]. **Only `apply_keyframes` and `retime_keyframes` accept the `{ type: 'PRESET', name }` shorthand; `animate_paint`, `animate_property` and `set_group_transform` need these raw coefficients — they silently downgrade an unrecognised easing shape to LINEAR (wrong motion, no error).** Preset equivalents: ease-in 0.42,0,1,1 · ease-out 0,0,0.58,1 · ease-in-out 0.42,0,0.58,1 · gentle-out 0.22,1,0.36,1 · snappy-out 0.16,1,0.3,1 · smooth-in-out 0.65,0,0.35,1 · overshoot-soft 0.34,1.56,0.64,1 · overshoot-hard 0.68,-0.55,0.265,1.55 · anticipate 0.22,-0.4,0.56,1.

tools.name: reorder_shape
tools.description: Restack a child shape or group relative to a sibling inside the same shape container — to fix internal card/icon order without rebuilding the layer. Z-order: `position: 'in_front_of'` draws the node ON TOP of the sibling, `'behind'` draws it under. Use `in_front_of`/`behind` (clear); `before`/`after` are legacy aliases that invert intuitively (`before` = on top).

position.description: `in_front_of` = on top of the sibling; `behind` = under it. (`before`=in_front_of, `after`=behind — legacy.)

tools.name: set_layer_time
tools.description:
Retime an existing layer on the timeline. Any combination of start_frame, end_frame, and timeline_offset can be set — omitted values stay as-is.

- `start_frame` / `end_frame`: when the layer is visible in the parent scene.
- `timeline_offset`: how far the layer's internal timeline is shifted (negative = play later). This is the stagger primitive — give each sibling a different offset.

Prefer this over `apply_keyframes` on opacity when the user asks to 'delay' or 'stagger' layers — this is cheaper, correct, and doesn't collide with existing opacity animations.

tools.name: retime_keyframes
tools.description:
Shift, scale, reverse, evenly distribute, or RE-EASE keyframes on one layer property WITHOUT rebuilding values. Use for timing/feel polish like "shift this 10 frames later", "make the bounce twice as fast", or "make it springier".

**To change the EASING / feel (springy, snappy, smoother, bouncy, more/less overshoot) use `operation: 'set_easing'` with `easing` — NOT apply_keyframes.** set_easing swaps only the easing curve and preserves every frame and value. Rewriting the animation via apply_keyframes forces you to restate all values and risks corrupting positions (e.g. collapsing a staggered word onto itself). For a multi-layer cascade (split-text letters, card grid), call set_easing once PER layer — each call is value-safe, so the layout cannot drift.

**Every operation reads the property's CURRENT keyframes, rewrites their frames, and puts the same values back — values are never touched by any operation.** The tool throws if the property has no keyframes yet (use `apply_keyframes` to create them first).

`operation`, and the parameters each one reads (all others are ignored):
- **`shift_frames`** — moves every keyframe by `offset` frames. Positive = LATER, negative = EARLIER. "shift this 10 frames later" = `{ operation: 'shift_frames', offset: 10 }`. **`offset` defaults to 0, so `{ operation: 'shift_frames' }` with no `offset` is schema-valid and does nothing** — always pass it. Frames are clamped at 0, so shifting earlier past the start piles those keyframes onto frame 0 and flattens that part of the motion; check the returned `frames`.
- **`scale_time`** — multiplies each keyframe's DISTANCE FROM THE ORIGIN by `scale`: `new = origin + (old - origin) * scale`. The origin is `start_frame` if given, otherwise the property's FIRST keyframe. `scale` must be greater than 0; zero and negative values are rejected before any keyframes change. `scale < 1` = faster/shorter, `scale > 1` = slower/longer. "make the bounce twice as fast" = `{ operation: 'scale_time', scale: 0.5 }`; "twice as slow" = `scale: 2`. `scale` defaults to 1 (no-op) — always pass it. The result is NOT rounded, so a scale that does not divide the spans evenly leaves keyframes on fractional frames (frame 7 × 0.5 = 3.5); prefer factors that land on whole frames.
- **`reverse`** — mirrors the frames inside a window: `new = start + end - old`, so the motion plays backwards while keeping the same span. The window defaults to the property's first→last keyframe; pass `start_frame`/`end_frame` to mirror inside a different window.
- **`distribute_evenly`** — respaces the EXISTING keyframes at equal intervals between `start_frame` and `end_frame` (defaults: first→last keyframe), keeping their order and values. Use it to kill uneven timing ("even out the spacing", "make the steps regular"). It does not add or remove keyframes.
- **`set_easing`** — replaces the easing curve on every keyframe of the property; frames and values are untouched. Requires `easing` (the call throws without it).

**RESPONSE:** returns `{ layer_id, property, operation, retimed, frames }`. `retimed` is how many keyframes were rewritten (unchanged from before — this operation never adds or drops keyframes) and `frames` is the full new frame list, sorted. **Check `frames` before saying done:** repeated values mean keyframes collided (clamping at 0, or a `scale` small enough to merge them) and that stretch of the animation is now flat.

offset.description: Frames to move every keyframe by, for operation 'shift_frames'. POSITIVE = later, NEGATIVE = earlier. Defaults to 0 (a silent no-op), so always pass it for that operation. Ignored by every other operation.

scale.description: Positive time multiplier for operation 'scale_time', applied to each keyframe's distance from the origin (`start_frame`, else the first keyframe). Must be greater than 0; invalid values are rejected without changing keyframes. 0.5 = twice as fast, 2 = twice as slow. Defaults to 1 (a silent no-op), so always pass it for that operation. Ignored by every other operation.

start_frame.description: Window start. For 'scale_time' this is the ORIGIN the scaling pivots around (keyframes at this frame do not move). For 'reverse' and 'distribute_evenly' it is the start of the frame window. Defaults to the property's FIRST existing keyframe. Ignored by 'shift_frames' and 'set_easing'.

end_frame.description: Window end for 'reverse' (the mirror is `start + end - frame`) and 'distribute_evenly' (the last keyframe lands here). Defaults to the property's LAST existing keyframe. Ignored by 'shift_frames', 'scale_time' and 'set_easing'.

easing.description:
Easing for operation 'set_easing' (required by it, ignored by every other operation). 'overshoot-soft'/'overshoot-hard' = springy/bouncy; 'snappy-out' = snappy; 'smooth-in-out' = smooth. Applied to the property's keyframes in place, values and frames untouched.

Accepts EITHER the bare preset name (`'gentle-out'`) OR the same object form `apply_keyframes` takes (`{ type: 'PRESET', name: 'gentle-out' }`, `{ type: 'LINEAR' }`, `{ type: 'CUBIC_BEZIER', x1, y1, x2, y2 }`) — carry whichever shape you already have, no translation needed.

anyOf.description: Explicit bezier control points [x1, y1, x2, y2]. **Only `apply_keyframes` and `retime_keyframes` accept the `{ type: 'PRESET', name }` shorthand; `animate_paint`, `animate_property` and `set_group_transform` need these raw coefficients — they silently downgrade an unrecognised easing shape to LINEAR (wrong motion, no error).** Preset equivalents: ease-in 0.42,0,1,1 · ease-out 0,0,0.58,1 · ease-in-out 0.42,0,0.58,1 · gentle-out 0.22,1,0.36,1 · snappy-out 0.16,1,0.3,1 · smooth-in-out 0.65,0,0.35,1 · overshoot-soft 0.34,1.56,0.64,1 · overshoot-hard 0.68,-0.55,0.265,1.55 · anticipate 0.22,-0.4,0.56,1.

Named curve — prefer this over hand-picked CUBIC_BEZIER coefficients. Presets expand to the exact bezier values server-side. Each maps to a motion PERSONALITY archetype — pick the one matching your Direction and use it consistently (see motion-design.md → Motion Personality):
- 'gentle-out' — PREMIUM archetype (elegant/luxury/minimal): smooth ease-out, 0% overshoot, ~350-600ms feel. The reveal default; spreads motion across the full duration.
- 'snappy-out' — CORPORATE archetype (clean/professional/dashboard): quick, decisive settle, 0-3% overshoot, ~200-400ms.
- 'overshoot-soft' / 'overshoot-hard' — PLAYFUL archetype (fun/bouncy/cute): pop-in / bouncy settle, 10-20% overshoot, ~150-300ms.
- 'anticipate' — PLAYFUL/ENERGETIC wind-up: pulls back before moving forward.
- 'ease-in-out' / 'smooth-in-out' — both ends, cinematic (neutral).
- 'ease-in' / 'ease-out' — CSS-standard, reliable neutral default.

tools.name: delete_layer
tools.description: Remove ONE layer from the scene by id. If the scene digest selection is non-empty and the user says 'delete this', 'remove it', 'delete selected', etc., use the selected layer id(s) with this tool. For multiple selected layers, call this tool once per selected id. Returns `{ layer_id, removed: true }`.

tools.name: create_mask
tools.description:
Add a mask to a layer. Masks clip the layer's visible content to an arbitrary shape — use for reveal wipes ('reveal from left'), clipping images/Lotties to a shape ('mask this image to a circle'), and any 'show only the part inside' request.

For the common shapes, pass one of the shorthands:

- `shape: "rectangle"` + `rect: { x, y, width, height }` — axis-aligned rectangle in LAYER-local coordinates.
- `shape: "ellipse"` + `ellipse: { cx, cy, width, height }` — center-defined ellipse, width/height being the bounding box. Plugin synthesizes a 4-point cubic bezier approximation (standard kappa constant).
- `shape: "path"` + `path: { points: [{vertex:{x,y}, inTan:{x,y}, outTan:{x,y}}...], closed: boolean }` — raw PathData for complex shapes.

Coords are LAYER-LOCAL — a rect at (0, 0, 100, 100) covers the top-left 100×100 of the layer's content, regardless of where the layer sits in the scene.

Optional `mode` defaults to 'add' (show only inside the mask). Pass 'subtract' to cut a hole. Optional `opacity` (0–100) controls mask opacity; it is not an enable/disable strength. For an ADD mask, opacity 0 makes the masked layer fully transparent and 100 shows the content inside the outline. For a SUBTRACT mask, opacity 0 cuts nothing and 100 fully cuts inside the outline. Use `remove_mask` to restore unmasked rendering.

**RESPONSE — this is the ONLY source of a mask id:** returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, shape, mode, opacity }`. `read_scene` does NOT list masks or mask ids, so if you need to address a specific mask later, keep `mask_id` from this response. Everything that takes a mask id also has a first-mask fallback, so a lost id is recoverable on single-mask layers: `update_mask` / `remove_mask` act on the FIRST mask when `mask_id` is omitted, and `animate_property` targets the first mask when both `target_id` and `target_index` are omitted.

Animate mask opacity/path with `animate_property({ layer_id, property: 'mask_opacity' | 'mask_path', ... })` — pass `target_id: mask_id` (or `target_index`) only when the layer has MORE THAN ONE mask; otherwise omit both and it uses the first one. `apply_keyframes` targets layer properties only and cannot reach masks. Note `mask_path` keyframe values are whole PathData objects (`{ points: [...], closed }`), not a width — build the full path for each keyframe.

Common recipes:
- 'reveal from left': rectangle mask at (0, 0, 0, layerH), then animate `mask_path` from a zero-width rect to a full-width one with `animate_property`.
- 'circle clip': ellipse mask, cx/cy = layer center, width/height = desired diameter.
- 'oval-vignette': ellipse mask slightly inset from layer bounds, opacity 0 → 100 animated with `animate_property` on `mask_opacity`.

rect.description: Required when `shape` is "rectangle"; omit for other mask shapes.

ellipse.description: Required when `shape` is "ellipse"; omit for other mask shapes.

path.description: Required when `shape` is "path"; omit for other mask shapes.

mode.description: Default 'add'. 'add' = show ONLY the content inside the mask outline (the normal clip/reveal). 'subtract' = cut a HOLE — hide the content inside the outline and show everything outside it.

opacity.description: Mask opacity, not an enable/disable strength. Default 100. For an ADD mask, 100 shows the content inside the outline and 0 makes the masked layer fully transparent. For a SUBTRACT mask, 100 fully cuts the content inside the outline and 0 cuts nothing. Use `remove_mask` to restore unmasked rendering.

tools.name: update_mask
tools.description:
Update an existing mask path, opacity, or mode. Use after create_mask when the reveal shape needs tuning without recreating the mask. Only the fields you pass change; omitted fields are left alone.

Returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, updated: { path, opacity, mode } }` — each `updated` flag reports whether that field was part of this call.

mask_id.description: Mask id from the `create_mask` response. Omit to update the layer's FIRST mask — `read_scene` does not list mask ids, so on a single-mask layer omitting this is the normal path. Errors with "mask not found" if the id is not on this layer.

path.description: Replacement mask outline, in LAYER-LOCAL coordinates.

opacity.description: Mask opacity. For an ADD mask, 100 shows inside the outline and 0 makes the masked layer fully transparent. For a SUBTRACT mask, 100 fully cuts inside and 0 cuts nothing. Use `remove_mask` to restore unmasked rendering. Omit to leave unchanged.

mode.description: 'add' = show ONLY the content inside the mask outline (the normal clip/reveal). 'subtract' = cut a HOLE — hide the content inside the outline and show everything outside it. Omit to leave the current mode unchanged.

tools.name: remove_mask
tools.description: Remove one mask from a layer. Pass mask_id when known; otherwise removes the first mask only. Returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, removed: true }`.

tools.name: set_matte
tools.description:
Apply a track/alpha matte: use another layer's alpha/shape as the visibility matte for this layer. This is THE premium-reveal primitive — what AE calls 'Alpha Matte'.

Typical flow:
1. User has (or you create) the layer to be revealed (the logo, image, text).
2. User has (or you create) a second layer whose shape defines the reveal region (a growing circle, a wipe rectangle, a word-shaped text layer).
3. Call `set_matte({ layer_id: target, matte_layer_id: matteSource })`.

The native tool sets `matteSource.isMatte = true` so the matte layer itself becomes invisible in the render while still defining the reveal region. Animate the matte source (position, scale, trim path, etc.) and the target layer is revealed accordingly.

Pass `inverted: true` to show the target OUTSIDE the matte shape instead of inside (inverted alpha matte).

Common recipes:
- 'reveal logo through a growing circle': create ellipse shape → set_matte with matte_layer_id = circle → apply_keyframes on circle.scale 0 → 100.
- 'text appears through a gradient sweep': create rectangle → set_matte → animate rectangle x across the text width.
- 'punch a hole': set_matte with inverted: true.

layer_id.description: The layer whose visibility will be gated by the matte.

matte_layer_id.description: The layer whose shape defines the matte region. The native tool flips its `isMatte` flag so it stops rendering as its own layer.

inverted.description: When true, show the target OUTSIDE the matte shape (subtract). Default false (show inside).

tools.name: remove_matte
tools.description: Clear the track matte from a layer.

tools.name: rename_node
tools.description: Rename a layer, shape, group, mask, or scene node by id. Use for cleanup and making generated structures understandable.

tools.name: set_layer_visibility
tools.description: Show or hide one active-scene layer.

tools.name: set_layer_lock
tools.description: Lock or unlock one active-scene layer.

tools.name: flip_layer
tools.description: Mirror a layer horizontally or vertically. Wraps `layer.flip(direction)`. Use for 'mirror this', 'flip horizontally', 'face the other way'. Works on any layer type.

tools.name: align_layer
tools.description:
**Use this as your first choice for centering or aligning layers to the scene.** Wraps Creator's own alignment math — the exact same path the property-panel 'align center' / 'align left' / 'align top' buttons run. Works reliably across text, shape, and image layers.

`horizontal-center` aligns the layer's visual bounds to the scene's horizontal midpoint; `vertical-center` to the vertical midpoint. For a fully-centered layer, emit BOTH in order: one tool call with `direction: 'horizontal-center'` and then one with `direction: 'vertical-center'`. Same for 'top-left' → `top` + `left`, and so on.

**Prefer this over `center_layer({ target })` unless you need to land on a NON-scene-center point** (e.g. a callout at (180, 380)). For brand-new centered text, prefer `create_text({ center_in_scene: true })` — that's even fewer calls.

**RESPONSE:** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. For text layers, `position` is intentionally omitted — `visual_center` is the only placement coordinate that matters.

tools.name: align_layers
tools.description:
Align a SET of existing layers to a shared edge derived from the set itself — the multi-layer counterpart of `align_layer` (which only aligns ONE layer to a SCENE edge). Use this to FIX a row/column you (or the user) hand-placed that came out ragged or misaligned: e.g. make a column of labels share a LEFT edge, or a row of icons share a TOP edge.

`edge`: which edge to make flush — `left`/`right`/`horizontal-center` (x-axis) or `top`/`bottom`/`vertical-center` (y-axis). Edge-anchored by each layer's RENDERED visual bounds (so text aligns by its real left/right edge, not its baseline anchor).

`to` (optional): the coordinate to align to — `min` (leftmost/topmost; default for left/top), `max` (default for right/bottom), `mean` (default for centers), `first` (the first layer's edge), or an explicit number. 

Guards: refuses layers with ANIMATED position (all-or-nothing) — align BEFORE animating, then `stagger_layers`. Returns `{ aligned, edge, axis, value, layer_ids }`.

layer_ids.description: The layers to align to each other (≥2).

to.description: Coordinate to align to: 'min' | 'max' | 'first' | 'mean' | a number. Omit for sensible defaults (min for left/top, max for right/bottom, mean for centers).

tools.name: layout
tools.description:
Lay out multiple items in a ROW or COLUMN with EVEN spacing and shared-edge alignment — in ONE call. **Use this instead of hand-placing positions** for any multi-item arrangement: nav menus, button rows, lists, label stacks, feature rows, and especially LEGENDS / swatch grids / spec-sheet rows / icon lists (a swatch legend = a column of `{swatch, label}` row-blocks — hand-placing those overlaps the label onto the swatch). It creates the items (or arranges existing layers), measures each rendered size, and computes even gaps + alignment so the result is correct by construction — no pixel math, no uneven gaps, no ragged edges.

`type`: `row` (horizontal) or `column` (vertical). Provide EITHER `items` (to create text/shapes) OR `layer_ids` (to arrange existing layers) — not both.

`gap` (default 24): the SINGLE even gap between items. `align` (cross-axis, default `center`): `start` = shared leading edge (left for a column, top for a row — this is how you get a left-aligned list), `center`, `end`. `origin` (default `scene-center`): where the whole block centers — `scene-center` / `top-center` / `bottom-center` / `{x,y}`.

Item kinds: `{ kind: 'text', text, font_size?, fill_color?, font_variant? }`, `{ kind: 'shape', shape, size, fill_color?, roundness?, points?, outer_radius?, inner_radius?, stroke? }`, `{ kind: 'layer', layer_id }`, or a NESTED `{ kind: 'block', type:'row'|'column', items:[…], gap?, align?, group? }` — a sub-layout the parent treats as one unit. Use a block to compose multi-row/column layouts in ONE call: e.g. a vertical list of icon+label rows where the icons all share a left edge and the labels all share another →
`layout({ type:'column', align:'start', gap:24, items:[
  { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[{kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:32,height:32}},{kind:'text',text:'Create account'}] },
  { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[…'Verify email'] },
  { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[…'Invite your team'] } ]})`.
The outer `column align:'start'` flushes each row-block's left edge, so all circles land on one x and all labels on another — no follow-up `align_layers`. A nested block takes `items` only (no `origin`/`layer_ids`); `group:true` on a block makes it one animatable precomp. Max nesting depth 3.

**Cards:** add `background:{ fill, roundness?, padding?, stroke?, shadow? }` to a block to drop a rounded panel sized to its content + padding BEHIND it — so a card = panel + content builds in ONE call (never create the content then bolt a panel on top). **`background` works on a block that CREATES its `items`, OR on the top-level `layout` call itself (it wraps the whole layout in one card panel)** — so build the card's content INSIDE the block (`items:[…]`), do NOT pre-create the text/shapes and then arrange them by `layer_ids` and try to wrap them. If you catch yourself doing `create_shape` (panel) + `reorder_layer` (behind) + `add_drop_shadow` around already-made content, STOP — that's the legacy bolt-on this `background` replaces; rebuild the content as `items` inside the block instead. With `group:true` the whole card becomes one animatable precomp you can slide/scale/fade as a unit. `fill` is required (use `fill:'none'` with a `stroke` for an outlined card); `padding` defaults to 24. E.g. a feature card: `{ kind:'block', type:'column', align:'center', gap:12, group:true, background:{ fill:{r:248,g:250,b:252}, roundness:16, padding:24, shadow:{} }, items:[ {kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:48,height:48}}, {kind:'text',text:'Fast'} ] }`.

Returns `items` (each with `layer_id`, `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`; a block item also has `kind:'block'` + `child_layer_ids`), `cascade_order` (flattened reading order of staggerable root layers — pass straight to `stagger_layers`), `evenness` (`main_gaps`, `uniform`), and `content_bounds`. Examples: a left-aligned nav = `layout({ type:'column', align:'start', items:[{kind:'text',text:'Home'},…] })`; a feature row = `layout({ type:'row', align:'center', items:[{kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:40,height:40}},{kind:'text',text:'Fast'}] })`.

tools.name: read_keyframes
tools.description:
Read the current keyframes on a layer's keyframe-tool properties. Use this whenever the user asks to TUNE, POLISH, or MODIFY an existing animation ('make the bounce snappier', 'slow down the fade', 'shift this 10 frames later', 'make the rotation smoother') — so you can see what's actually there before changing it, instead of rebuilding from scratch.

Without `property`, returns a map of the core properties handled by `apply_keyframes` (`position`, `scale`, `rotation`, `opacity`, `fill_color`, trim path fields, and `stroke_width`). With `property`, returns just that explicit core or extended property. Extended properties such as masks, shape paths, gradients, text animator fields, and time mapping must be named explicitly; they are not included in the bulk read.

For static (non-animated) properties, `is_animated` is false and `static_value` is returned instead of keyframes.

**For `position` on a TEXT layer, `static_value` is the RAW transform (baseline / box-origin anchor) — NOT the visual center. To animate a text position relative to its rest (the only safe way), keyframe from THIS `static_value`, not from `visual_center`. For a settle-into-place entrance, prefer `animate_entrance`, which reads this for you.**

Easing in returned keyframes comes through as the raw stored shape: `{ type: "LINEAR" }` or `{ type: "CUBIC_BEZIER", x1, y1, x2, y2 }`. (Named presets are expanded at write-time, so reads only see the resolved bezier coefficients.)

property.description: Optional — restrict to one core or extended keyframe-tool property. Omit to read all core keyframe-tool properties on the layer.

tools.name: copy_animation
tools.description:
Copy keyframes from one layer's core keyframe-tool properties onto another. The classic use: 'match this layer's animation to the others,' 'copy the rotation from the big triangle to the small one,' 'give this the same entrance as that one.'

By default, animated core properties from `apply_keyframes` are copied — pass `properties` to restrict. Extended `animate_property` fields such as masks, shape paths, gradients, text animator fields, and time mapping are not copied by this tool. Pass `frame_offset` to shift all copied keyframes by N frames, which stacks with this tool for manual staggers (e.g. call copy_animation for each sibling with a different offset).

`clear_first_on_target` (default true) replaces any existing keyframes on the target's matching property; pass false to merge.

Properties that don't exist on the target layer type (e.g., `fill_color` on a text layer) are skipped with a note in the response rather than erroring the whole call.

properties.description: Optional — which core keyframe-tool properties to copy. Omit to copy all animated core properties on the source.

frame_offset.description: Shift every copied keyframe's `frame` by this many frames. Negative = play earlier, positive = play later. Default 0.

clear_first_on_target.description: When true (default), clear each property's existing keyframes on the target before copying. When false, merge with existing.

tools.name: list_scenes
tools.description:
List every scene in the current project plus which one is active. Cheap read. Use when the user refers to scenes by name ('switch to the outro', 'work on the vertical') so you can find the right `scene_id`, or when deciding whether to create a new scene vs. switch to an existing one.

Returns active scene id, and for each scene: id, name, size, framerate, duration, layer_count, and is_nestable (whether the scene can be used as a source for a nested scene layer).

tools.name: create_scene
tools.description:
Create a new scene (a.k.a. composition / artboard) in the project. Use for 'make a vertical variant', 'add a second scene for the outro', 'new 1080×1920 version', 'start fresh on a new composition'.

All fields optional — omit to inherit defaults. If size is omitted, Creator uses its default (typically 1920×1080). Provide explicit size when the user asks for a specific aspect ratio (9:16 → 1080×1920, 1:1 → 1080×1080, etc.).

**IMPORTANT**: `activate` defaults to true, meaning the newly created scene becomes the active scene. Any layer IDs you had from before (in history or from a recent read_scene) are INVALID in the new active scene — they belong to the previous scene. Call `read_scene` immediately after this tool before using any layer-targeting tool. If the user wants a new scene without switching, pass `activate: false` and the current scene stays active.

name.description: Scene name as shown in Creator's scene picker.

framerate.description: Frames per second. Default: Creator's fallback.

activate.description: Switch to the new scene immediately (default true). Set false to create but keep the current scene active.

tools.name: switch_scene
tools.description:
Switch Creator's active scene. Provide either `scene_id` (exact) or `name` (exact or case-insensitive substring match across scenes). Use `list_scenes` first if you're not sure what's available.

**IMPORTANT**: After this tool runs, any layer_id from prior turns is INVALID — those layers live in the scene you just switched away from. Call `read_scene` before using any layer-targeting tool on the new active scene. If you switched temporarily into a selected precomp/source scene, switch back to the original active scene before ending the turn.

name.description: Scene name. Exact first, then case-insensitive substring. Errors if 0 or more than 1 match.

tools.name: set_current_frame
tools.description: Move the active scene's playhead to a specific frame. Use this after creating reveal/draw-on/fade-in animations where frame 0 is intentionally invisible (`trim_end: 0`, opacity 0, offscreen position) so the Creator canvas is left on a representative visible frame. This changes the editor preview frame only; it does not add animation keyframes or alter layer timing.

frame.description: Scene frame to show in Creator. Creator clamps to the scene range.

add_to_history.description: Whether this navigation should enter undo history. Default false; leave false for Motion Copilot preview positioning.

tools.name: set_scene_background
tools.description:
Set the PREVIEW background color of the active scene. **This is preview-only — the color is NOT exported with the final animation; exports always have a transparent background.** Use this whenever you want to see how the design reads against a specific surface (e.g. dark mode preview, brand tint preview, contrast check for white-on-X) WITHOUT polluting the scene with a background rectangle layer.

**Strongly prefer this over creating a background SHAPE LAYER.** Motion-design convention: animations float on transparency so they can be composited anywhere. Adding a background rectangle layer adds noise, exports unwanted color, and forces the user to delete it if they want to use the animation on a different surface. The only reasons to add a real background SHAPE LAYER are: (1) a gradient or multi-stop background that's part of the design, (2) a contrast issue that can't be solved any other way, (3) the user EXPLICITLY says 'add a background layer' or similar.

For every other case (the user says 'on a dark background', 'against a navy backdrop', 'preview on cream', etc.) use this tool — it changes the scene's preview color, leaves the final animation transparent.

**REQUIRED, not optional:** when the scene has no background AND you place near-white (luminance > 0.5, e.g. #f8fafc / #ffffff) full-bleed text or fills, you MUST call this in the SAME turn with a dark color (Slate-900 {r:15,g:23,b:42}) — the default preview is white and light text would be invisible. Button labels on a dark button fill are self-contained and do NOT trigger this; only full-bleed text on the canvas does.

tools.name: set_scene_settings
tools.description: Update the active scene size, framerate, duration, and/or origin point. Use for prompts like "make this 1080x1920", "make it 60fps", or "extend to 8 seconds".

tools.name: create_scene_layer
tools.description:
Place an existing NESTABLE scene/precomp into the active scene as a SceneLayer (nested composition / component / precomp). Use this for professional card, panel, logo, or UI units only when `list_scenes` reports the source scene has `is_nestable: true`.

Important: newly created top-level scenes that report `is_nestable: false`; those cannot be used as scene-layer sources. Do not create a fresh scene and immediately try to place it unless `list_scenes` confirms it is nestable. For generated cards/panels, prefer a single grouped ShapeLayer when no nestable source exists.

Provide `source_scene_id` from `list_scenes`, or `source_scene_name` if unique. The layer is created in the current active scene. The source scene cannot be the current active scene — switch to the parent scene first. After creation, animate the returned `layer_id` like any other layer, and apply `set_matte` to this one layer for viewport clipping.

source_scene_name.description: Source scene name. Exact first, then case-insensitive substring. Errors if 0 or more than 1 match.

name.description: Optional name for the created SceneLayer.

scale.description: Optional initial scale in percent. Applied after layer creation.

tools.name: break_scene_layer
tools.description: Destructively break an active-scene scene/precomp layer into independent editable layers. Use only when the user explicitly asks to break apart, detach, ungroup, or extract a nested scene. Do not use for normal edits to a precomp/scene layer contents; switch to the source scene and edit there instead.

tools.name: apply_bounce
tools.description:
Drop or lift a layer with physics-correct bounce keyframes. **Use this for any prompt mentioning bounce / drop / fall / land / gravity**. Computes a parametric trajectory: each successive bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration, which is the part hand-tuned bounces always miss (uniform-timing decay reads as wrong).

**Position-only by design.** Squash-and-stretch is a separate concern — call `apply_squash` afterward if the user explicitly asked for a 'playful' / 'cartoon' / 'springy' bounce. A bare 'bounce' should not deform the layer's scale.

Defaults pick a 'snappy but natural' bounce. Tune `elasticity` and `gravity` for feel:
- elasticity 0.4 (stiff, settles fast) → 0.85 (cartoony, lots of bounces)
- gravity 1500 (floaty) → 12000 (heavy)
- max_bounces 4 is visible; >6 is sub-pixel

Returns the impact frame numbers in the response under `impact_frames`. These frames are non-uniform (each bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration). Any follow-up tool that targets impacts — `apply_squash`, `apply_coupled_shadow` — **must consume this exact array from the response**. Do NOT estimate, do NOT recompute from elasticity/gravity, do NOT call those tools in parallel with `apply_bounce` (they need the response in scope). Sequence: `apply_bounce` → read response → `apply_squash` / `apply_coupled_shadow` with `impact_frames` from that response.

axis.description: Position axis to bounce on. Default 'y' (gravity-driven drop).

from.description: Starting value for the chosen axis. Defaults to the layer's current static position on that axis.

to.description: Resting value the bounce settles to. For a 'drop and bounce', this is the floor y (greater than `from`). For a 'lift in', it's the peak y (less than `from`). Required.

elasticity.description: Energy retained per bounce, 0-0.99. 0.65 is the playful default.

start_frame.description: Frame at which the bounce begins. Default 0.

clear_first.description: Replace existing position keyframes. Default true.

tools.name: apply_squash
tools.description:
Add squash-and-stretch scale keyframes at specified impact frames. **Only call this when the user explicitly asks for 'playful' / 'cartoon' / 'springy' / 'squashy' / 'with squash and stretch' on top of a bounce.** A bare 'bounce' should NOT include squash — leave the layer's scale untouched.

**CRITICAL — `impact_frames` MUST be the literal array returned by `apply_bounce`'s response. NEVER invent them, NEVER estimate them, NEVER guess at multiples of a frame number.** This tool is SEQUENTIALLY DEPENDENT on `apply_bounce`: emit `apply_bounce` first, READ its response's `impact_frames` array, then pass that exact array into this tool's `impact_frames` parameter. Do not emit both calls in parallel — `apply_squash` is meaningless without the bounce response in scope. The failure mode if you invent frames: squash fires AFTER the ball has already come to rest (impact frames must land exactly on the bounce arcs, which are non-uniform because each bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration — you cannot derive them from elasticity/gravity by hand).

Given the impact frames (always from `apply_bounce`'s response), emits a 5-keyframe envelope per impact: anticipation stretch (taller, narrower) → squash at impact (wider, shorter) → rebound stretch → settle. Decays the squash strength on successive impacts so the squash fades out as the bounce dies.

The scale.x/scale.y inversion is built in (squash widens X, narrows Y). Don't try to add this manually with apply_keyframes — the timing windows have to align with the bounce arcs or the squash flickers between bounces.

impact_frames.description: Frames where squash should fire. Use the `impact_frames` array returned by `apply_bounce`. Skipping the first impact for a 'bounces but doesn't squash on first contact' feel is fine.

ratio.description: Squash extent at the FIRST impact. 1.15 = subtle, 1.3 = playful, 1.5 = cartoon. Default 1.3.

decay_per_impact.description: Squash strength multiplier per successive impact. Default 0.7 — preserves visible squash for ~3 bounces.

min_spacing_frames.description: Skip impacts whose preceding/following bounce is shorter than this many frames (their squash window would overlap neighbors). Default 5.

clear_first.description: Replace existing scale keyframes. Default true.

tools.name: apply_coupled_shadow
tools.description:
Animate an existing shadow layer to track a bouncing object. **Always use this for shadows under bouncing balls** — it solves all five shadow bugs (A: position pinned at ball center, B: shadow wider than object, C: inverted scale direction, D: copying ball.scale onto shadow, E: redundant static keyframes) by computing every value from the ball's existing position keyframes via the rule:

`shadow.position.y = ball.y_at_rest + ball_radius` (CENTER, not top)
`shadow.scale.x = widthRatio × ball_diameter` (interpolates between apex and impact ratios; flat `scale.y`)
`shadow.opacity = inverse of altitude` (impact = brightest, apex = faintest)

**Two-layer stacked-solid fill.** A single solid black ellipse reads as a sticker; a radial-gradient ellipse currently can't export with per-stop alpha. Create TWO shadow ellipses (both circular at natural size, same dark slate solid fill `{r:15, g:23, b:42}`) and call `apply_coupled_shadow` once on each: an Outer 'Shadow Edge' layer (`width_ratio_at_impact: 1.35, width_ratio_at_apex: 0.6, opacity_at_impact: 0.30, opacity_at_apex: 0.10`) and an Inner 'Shadow Core' layer (`width_ratio_at_impact: 0.9, width_ratio_at_apex: 0.4, opacity_at_impact: 0.65, opacity_at_apex: 0.25`). Create the Outer FIRST so the Inner (created LAST) lands on TOP of it (Creator inserts new layers at the top of the stack).

**REQUIRED FOLLOW-UPS — do not skip:**
1. Call `add_blur` on EACH shadow layer to soften the edge. Use `sigma ≈ ball_diameter × 0.15` (e.g. 12 for an 80px ball, cap ~30). Without blur the shadow reads as a hard ellipse, not as a penumbra.
2. Call `reorder_layer` on EACH shadow layer with `position: 'behind'` and `sibling_layer_id` = the ball's id, to push each shadow BEHIND the ball. New layers ship at the top of the render stack; the shadow needs to be sent back. Without this the shadow paints over the ball.

See `motion-patterns.md` → 'Shadow fill' for the full recipe.

Reads the ball's animated position to derive `restY` (max y) and impact frames automatically. The shadow ellipse is auto-resized to `ball_diameter × ball_diameter` natural size so scale percentages render at the right physical width — you don't have to compute scale = target_width / natural_width.

Prerequisite: the ball must already have animated position (run `apply_bounce` on it first), and both the ball and the shadow must be ellipse SHAPE_LAYERS. **Create the shadow ellipse with CIRCULAR natural size — `{width: ball_diameter, height: ball_diameter}`. Do NOT pre-flatten the shape (e.g. height=24 for an 80px ball).** The flat-on-the-floor look is produced by this tool keyframing a low `scale.y` constant; if you pre-flatten the shape, the blur falloff zone falls outside the visible ellipse and the user sees a flat dark band. The shadow's fill is preserved through this tool (only size + position + scale + opacity are touched), so apply the fill via `set_fill` BEFORE calling this.

ball_layer_id.description: The bouncing ball layer (must have animated position).

shadow_layer_id.description: The shadow ellipse layer. Will be resized to ball_diameter × ball_diameter and have its position + scale + opacity keyframed.

width_ratio_at_impact.description: Shadow width at impact, as a multiplier of ball diameter. 1.0 = matches ball, 1.1 = slightly wider (default), 1.3 = noticeably wider. Never > 1.5 or it stops looking like the ball's shadow.

width_ratio_at_apex.description: Shadow width at apex, as a multiplier of ball diameter. 0.45 default — visibly shrunk but not a dot.

flatness.description: Shadow vertical extent as a multiplier of ball diameter. Default 0.3. Stays constant — the shadow doesn't pulse vertically.

opacity_at_impact.description: 0-1 ratio. Default 0.75 (75%). Bug guard: pass a ratio, NOT a percentage — values > 1 throw.

clear_first.description: Replace existing scale + opacity keyframes on the shadow. Default true.
